item.content:encoded:
Good morning! The NBA season is around the corner, and Portland Trail Blazers forward Deni Avdija is already reminding fans why he became the NBA’s first Israeli All-Star last season.
Avdija dropped a team-high 23 points in his preseason debut on Wednesday, with two rebounds and two assists in just 21 minutes.
The season tips off on Oct. 20.
Max Fried’s very bittersweet week
New York Yankees ace Max Fried took the mound Wednesday as the Bronx Bombers looked to stave off elimination against the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
It didn’t work.
The Yankees lost, 4-3, and were swept by their division rivals. Despite the low-scoring games, the series was never particularly close. Fried allowed four runs — including two home runs — in 5 2/3 innings, while the Yankees’ offense remained quiet. (Rowdy Tellez and the Atlanta Braves were also eliminated on Wednesday.) 
It’s another unfortunate chapter in Fried’s postseason career. His 5.11 career ERA in the playoffs is the worst in MLB history among pitchers with 75+ innings pitched.
But there’s a silver lining for Fried, who is set to become a father any day now.
Fried, who is typically on the private side when it comes to his personal life, confirmed before the game that his girlfriend, the former University of Southern California volleyball star Reni Meyer-Whalley, was due to give birth to the couple’s first child this week.
“I’d not like to get too into the personal stuff, but yeah, that’s true,” Fried said on Tuesday when asked about the pregnancy.
“I’ve got a real supportive family that understands that this is my job,” he added. “And it’s not going to affect what happens tomorrow.”
So the Yankees may be eliminated, but at least Fried will have a happy distraction this offseason. Mazel tov!
Halftime report
WE MEET AGAIN. Israel and Ireland played their second soccer match in as many weeks last Sunday, and it was just as tense as the first one. Irish players again wore black armbands, declined handshakes and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem. This time, the drama spilled off the pitch, too, with Israeli journalists clashing with Ireland’s football association at a heated press conference. Here’s more.
VOTE EARLY AND OFTEN. As the year draws to a close, the International Jewish Sports Hall of Fame is holding a fan vote for the Jewish athletes and performances of the year — from Deni Avdija’s breakout season and Jack Hughes’ heroics at the Olympics to Amit Elor and Jessica Fox’s dominance on the international stage. Cast your votes right here.
WELCOME BACK. Former college basketball star Dan Grunfeld is returning to his alma mater, Stanford University, as the men’s basketball team’s new general manager and assistant coach. After leading Stanford to three NCAA tournaments (including as a No. 1 seed in 2004), Grunfeld played in the NBA Summer League and abroad in Germany, Spain and Israel. He is the son of former NBA player and general manager Ernie Grunfeld, the only known child of Holocaust survivors to play in the league. Dan chronicles his family’s story in his book, “By the Grace of the Game: The Holocaust, a Basketball Legacy, and an Unprecedented American Dream.”
Jews in sports to watch this weekend (all times ET)
Hockey
Jeremy Swayman and the Boston Bruins host the Philadelphia Flyers Saturday at 1 p.m. Jack and Luke Hughes and the New Jersey Devils host Zeev Buium, Max Sasson and the Vancouver Canucks Saturday at 3:30 p.m. Zach Hyman, Jake Walman, Devon Levi and the Edmonton Oilers face coach Ryan Warsofsky’s San Jose Sharks Saturday at 4 p.m. Adam Fox and the New York Rangers host the Canucks Sunday at 6 p.m.
Soccer
Liel Abada, Idan Toklomati and Charlotte FC host Ran Binyamin and FC Dallas Saturday at 7:30 p.m. At the same time, Tai Baribo and D.C. United face Inter Miami, DeAndre Yedlin and Real Salt Lake take on the Philadelphia Union and Matt Turner, Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and the New England Revolution host the Seattle Sounders. Daniel Edelman and St. Louis City host the LA Galaxy Sunday at 7 p.m. In the English Championship, Manor Solomon and West Ham United host Queens Park Rangers today at 3 p.m.
Golf
Max Homa, Max Greyserman and David Lipsky are all competing at the Baycurrent Classic this weekend in Yokohama, Japan.
Racing
Aston Martin driver Lance Stroll races in the Formula One Singapore Grand Prix Sunday at 8 a.m.
As the Year Turns, Support the Journalism You Trust. JTA covers the stories shaping Jewish life around the world — with the depth this moment calls for. As you reflect on the year ahead, consider a gift that keeps independent Jewish journalism strong.

item.content:encoded:
Several minutes after both the predictable and unthinkable — another team celebrating on the Yankees’ home turf, this time the Rays after sweeping through the ALDS — three Yankees lingered on the top step of the dugout. They stared. They absorbed. They stored what will be used as fuel.
Paul Blackburn peeled off the railing and began making his way to the clubhouse. Soon after, Aaron Judge followed.




Access the Yankees beat like never before

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
And finally, the last Yankee to force himself from watching the revolting sight was the youngest: George Lombard Jr.
“I’m going to have to learn from it and keep this feeling with it and use that in the work next year,” Lombard said after the Yankees were eliminated Wednesday night in The Bronx. “… It sucks. It hurts. There’s a lot of things that go into it, but yeah, it’s definitely a feeling that you don’t want to feel after your last game.
“It’s definitely going to be on my mind a lot.”
The Yankees will not fondly remember 2026, when Judge and Giancarlo Stanton missed much of the season, their replacements did not adequately replace them and yet another campaign ended in disappointment, but it is at least possible it will be recalled as the year Lombard earned his shot.
A year that started in Double-A Somerset, where Lombard did not even last a month, ended as the everyday, playoff shortstop for the Yankees.
He showed flashes of brilliance defensively, and his fourth-inning highlight — in which he charged a chopper that had leaped over Max Fried, barehanded and slung a throw to cut down Junior Caminero — might have been remembered if the game finished differently. He also showed that he is 21 years old, both with his six-game error streak and in being part of the Game 2 defensive meltdown.
Offensively, he performed better than expected. The Yankees would welcome further steps, but a prospect known more for his glove and headiness hit .237 with a .699 OPS in his first 42 games before holding his own in October.
Lombard’s first playoff run, albeit brief, finished at 6-for-18 (.333) with six singles and four strikeouts. On Wednesday, he was a bright spot in stroking a hard-hit single, adding another on a slow roller to third and later walking, using an automated ball-strike system challenge — which has been a strength of his — to earn the trip to first.
“It was definitely a good experience for the first year,” said Lombard, who replaced Anthony Volpe and José Caballero at shortstop in early August. “I’m going to take everything with me because it’s not the way we want to end going forward.”
There is little known about the Yankees’ 2027 infield. Can they really bring back Ryan McMahon, who is owed $16 million for next season, made a costly error in Game 2, was benched in Game 3 and simply did not hit enough this season?
Is Jazz Chisholm Jr., who also was benched for the elimination game, a goner as a free agent? Are the Yankees serious about Luis García Jr. possibly getting work at second base, which would open first for Ben Rice? Is Paul Goldschmidt, who wants to keep playing, still an option as a lefty-killer at first? Where do Volpe and Caballero fit?
The best bet among the group is that Lombard, a 2023 first-round pick whose first taste of major league life included more promise than problems, will be back at shortstop.
And motivated.
“Definitely a lot to take from it,” said Lombard, who was particularly upset about Judge, Stanton and Goldschmidt coming up short of a title. “It just sucks to go out like this.”

item.content:encoded:
Oct 8, 2026, 11:35 AM ET
New York Yankees impending free-agent first baseman/designated hitter Paul Goldschmidt has expressed a desire to keep playing at age 39 in 2027, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. It is unclear if the Yankees will make an effort to re-sign the former MVP and seven-time All-Star in the offseason. Goldy had a nice bounce-back campaign in 2026 in his 16th year in the big leagues after he hit just 10 homers and drove in 45 runs in 146 games in 2025 in his first year in pinstripes. In 105 regular-season games across 380 plate appearances this year, Goldschmidt hit .252/.313/.452 with a .765 OPS, 18 home runs, 52 RBI, and 44 runs scored for the Yankees. He went hitless in eight plate appearances with two walks and a run scored in four postseason games for New York this year. Goldschmidt is obviously no longer in his prime and is no longer an everyday player, but he should still attract interest across the league for his ability to hit lefties. In 183 plate appearances against southpaws in 2026, he hit .299 (47-for-157) with 11 of his 18 home runs and 24 RBI.--Keith Hernandez
Source: New York Daily News - Gary Phillips
More Recent News
Oct 8, 2026, 11:28 AM ET
Tampa Bay Rays closer Bryan Baker shut the door in his team's 4-3 win over the New York Yankees in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless ninth inning with two strikeouts. Baker was a key part of Tampa Bay's three-game sweep of New York, logging saves in all three games while allowing just one baserunner to reach. The 31-year-old emerged as one of the best closers in baseball during the regular season, recording a 1.44 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 63 strikeouts and 41 saves across 62 1/3 innings (65 games). Heading into the American League Championship Series, Baker's dominance at the end of games gives Tampa Bay a significant advantage if it can get an early lead on its opponents.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Jakob Marsee Having UCL Repair With Internal Brace


Keith Hernandez




Oct 8, 2026, 11:24 AM ET
Miami Marlins outfielder Jakob Marsee (elbow) will get a UCL repair with an internal brace of his left elbow on Monday, according to Christina De Nicola of MLB.com. The estimated return-to-play timeline for Marsee is around six months. Marsee battled through elbow issues down the stretch in 2026 in his first full season in the majors with Miami. In his first taste of the big leagues in 2025, Marsee hit .292 (61-for-209) with five home runs, 33 RBI, 14 stolen bases, and 28 runs scored in 55 games and 234 plate appearances. In 155 games and 616 plate appearances this year, Marsee slashed .231/.348/.359 with a .706 OPS, 11 home runs, 41 RBI, 23 stolen bases, and 83 runs scored for the Fish. The 25-year-old former sixth-round pick by the San Diego Padres in 2022 from Central Michigan University has a very intriguing power/speed profile as an outfielder in all fantasy leagues, but his availability for Opening Day in 2027 could be in question, depending on how he fares during his rehab after going under the knife early next week.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Christina De Nicola
Oct 8, 2026, 11:21 AM ET
Milwaukee Brewers outfielder Garrett Mitchell had a big game in his team's 3-1, series-clinching win over the San Diego Padres in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday. At the plate, Mitchell went two-for-four with a triple, an RBI, and a run scored. In the field, Mitchell robbed Padres third baseman Manny Machado of what would have been a game-tying two-run home run in the eighth inning. The 28-year-old Mitchell was finally able to stay mostly healthy in 2026, hitting .262/.354/.416 with 11 home runs, 65 RBI, 74 runs scored, and 14 stolen bases across 531 plate appearances in the regular season. He was productive in the NLDS as well, logging four hits, three runs scored, an RBI, and a stolen base across 15 at-bats.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Hagen Smith Opening Game 4 of ALDS on Thursday


Keith Hernandez




Oct 8, 2026, 11:15 AM ET
Chicago White Sox rookie left-hander Hagen Smith will serve as the opener in Game 4 of the American League Division Series on Thursday at home against the division-rival Cleveland Guardians, according to Scott Merkin of MLB.com. The 23-year-old former fifth overall pick in 2024 from the University of Arkansas made 18 appearances (only one start) in his major-league debut during the 2026 regular season, posting a nice 1.29 ERA (2.35 FIP) and 0.96 WHIP with 41 strikeouts and 16 walks in 28 innings pitched. The talented young southpaw has already thrown 6 1/3 innings in his first experience in the playoffs, too, allowing just one earned run on three hits while walking five and striking out six. He started Game 1 of the ALDS against Cleveland and threw 2 2/3 shutout innings with three walks and four strikeouts in the team's 3-0 victory before allowing a run with two walks and a strikeout in two-thirds of an inning in Wednesday's Game 3 loss. Smith will probably have a short leash as the White Sox try to close out the best-of-five series, with right-hander Erick Fedde potentially piggybacking Smith in Chicago. In three relief appearances against the Guardians during the regular season, Smith allowed two earned runs with six walks and eight strikeouts in 5 2/3 innings pitched.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Scott Merkin
Victor Mesa Jr. Homers in ALDS-Clinching Win


Will Brady




Oct 8, 2026, 11:14 AM ET
Tampa Bay Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr. was one of the stars of his team's 4-3 win in Game 3 of the American League Division Series over the New York Yankees, hitting a two-run home run off Yankees left-hander Max Fried. Mesa Jr.'s home run was his only hit of the night, but it gave the Rays a 4-2 lead in the sixth inning that they would ultimately never give back. Across 262 plate appearances in the regular season, Mesa Jr. hit .260/.327/.498 with 14 home runs, 34 RBI, 37 runs scored, and nine stolen bases. After starting the year in the minors, the 25-year-old has emerged as an everyday corner outfielder for Tampa Bay and provides another dynamic power/speed bat for the Rays. If Mesa Jr. can get hot, he could help power a deep postseason run.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 10:01 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers closer Edwin Diaz picked up his second save in as many nights on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless ninth inning with a strikeout in his team's 4-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the National League Division Series. Diaz missed most of the 2026 regular season due to elbow and neck injuries. However, he's been dominant since returning from the injured list in mid-September. Diaz allowed just two baserunners while notching nine strikeouts in his final five innings pitched of the regular season, and he's now logged low-stress saves in each of his first two appearances of the playoffs. With Diaz rounding into form, Los Angeles' bullpen looks like a major strength heading into the National League Championship Series.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:52 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians left-hander Foster Griffin was dominant in a bulk relief appearance in his team's 9-3 win over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday. Griffin followed Cleveland opener Daniel Espino and allowed two hits and one earned run while striking out seven across 2 2/3 innings of work. The 31-year-old was used exclusively as a starting pitcher during the regular season, posting a 15-6 record with a 3.60 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, and 158 strikeouts across 172 2/3 innings (31 starts) split between the Guardians and the Washington Nationals. However, Griffin struggled mightily late in the year, pitching to a 5.05 ERA in the second half and a 6.87 ERA across 18 1/3 innings in September. If Griffin can rediscover his early-season form in a bullpen role, he could help Cleveland mount a comeback in the ALDS.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:43 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians outfielder Jo Adell had a big night in his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday, going 2-for-4 with a walk and three RBI. With the game tied 1-1 in the third inning, Adell put the Guardians ahead for good with a three-run triple off of White Sox left-hander Hagen Smith. Across 660 regular-season plate appearances split between the Guardians and the Los Angeles Angels, Adell hit .240/.298/.401 with 23 home runs, 94 RBI, 70 runs scored, and five stolen bases. He was better with Cleveland than he was with Los Angeles, posting a .740 OPS across 204 trips to the plate after the Guardians acquired him at the trade deadline. Adell has notched a couple of key hits for Cleveland in the ALDS and now has four RBI across the first three games of the series.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:32 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages had the key hit in his team's 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday, logging a go-ahead two-run single off Braves right-hander Robert Suarez in the seventh inning. Pages finished the game with two hits and two RBI in three at-bats. The 25-year-old was a critical piece of the Dodgers lineup during the regular season, hitting .274 with 23 home runs, 85 RBI, 75 runs scored, and 13 stolen bases. However, Pages struggled mightily during the Dodgers' run to the 2025 World Series, notching just four hits in 55 postseason plate appearances. After his big night on Wednesday, Pages has already logged four hits in just 15 plate appearances in the 2026 playoffs.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:19 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians right-hander Cade Smith was lights out to secure his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday. Smith entered the game in the eighth inning and recorded the final six outs, logging five strikeouts without allowing a single baserunner. The 27-year-old was one of the best closers in baseball during the regular season, pitching to a 1.95 ERA and 0.96 WHIP with 107 strikeouts and 41 saves across 74 innings (69 games). Smith has been dominant so far in the Division Series as well, as he's yet to allow a hit or a walk in his four innings of work. If Cleveland is going to mount a comeback in the series, it will likely need Smith to continue his dominance.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:11 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians third baseman Jose Ramirez was one of the stars of his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series. In five plate appearances, Ramirez recorded a double, a triple, a walk, two RBI, two runs scored, and a stolen base. With Cleveland leading 5-3 in the 8th inning, it was Ramirez's two-run triple that sealed the win for the Guardians and kept the series alive to see Game 4. The 34-year-old battled through injuries and underperformance in 2026, hitting .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs, 53 RBI, 71 runs scored, and 37 stolen bases across 544 plate appearances. Ramirez also got off to a slow start in the postseason, going hitless in his first eight trips to the plate against the White Sox. If Cleveland is going to rally all the way back from two games down in the ALDS, it will need Ramirez to stay hot in Games 4 and 5.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Robert Gasser Starting Game 4 of NLDS Against Padres


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 8:08 PM ET
Milwaukee Brewers left-hander Robert Gasser will start for the Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday night at Petco Park against the San Diego Padres, according to Brewers reporter Sophia Minnaert. It will be Gasser's first career postseason start after throwing 2 2/3 innings of relief in the playoffs for the Brew Crew last year. The 27-year-old southpaw went 5-5 on the season with a 3.87 ERA (4.24 FIP) and 1.19 WHIP with a career-high 103 strikeouts and 35 walks in 109 1/3 innings across 21 appearances (20 starts). The problem for Gasser is that he has not made a start in almost two weeks, so he could be a bit rusty. Manager Pat Murphy will surely have a short hook on the young left-hander as the Brewers look to close the best-of-five series out in San Diego. Gasser was outstanding down the stretch in 2026, allowing two earned runs or fewer in each of his last six starts, walking 12 and striking out 31 in 32 1/3 innings during that span. He did not face the Padres at all during the regular season, which could give him a bit of an advantage.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Sophia Minnaert
Mason Miller Back From the Paternity List for Game 4


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 8:03 PM ET
The San Diego Padres announced on Wednesday that they returned right-handed closer Mason Miller from the paternity list, taking the place on the National League Division Series roster of left-handed reliever Wandy Peralta. Miller blew a two-inning save in Game 2 of the series in Milwaukee against the Brewers and was then unavailable for the win in Game 3 at Petco Park on Tuesday night. It is great news for the Padres, who did not have left-handed high-leverage reliever Adrian Morejon on Tuesday due to a left-shoulder issue. The Padres had to go to Game 1 starter, right-hander Michael King, for the two-inning save with both Miller and Morejon unavailable. It is uncertain if Morejon will be able to pitch late in the game in another must-win contest on Wednesday in Game 4, but the Padres will at least have their stud closer back in the fold. The two-time All-Star was lights-out during the regular season, his first full season with the Friars, posting a 1.67 ERA (1.17 FIP), 0.900 WHIP, a career-high and league-high 38 saves, a career-high 129 strikeouts, and 26 walks in just 70 innings pitched. With their season on the line, expect manager Craig Stammen to be aggressive in his usage of Miller if Game 4 is close in the later innings, even though he showed command issues in the ninth on Sunday in Milwaukee.--Keith Hernandez
Source: San Diego Padres
Miguel Rojas Not Worried About Back/Hip Injury


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 12:28 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers veteran infielder Miguel Rojas (back, hip) said he felt some tightness in his left lower-back/hip area during a swing in Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday against the hosting Atlanta Braves before he was pulled mid at-bat, according to Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic. However, Rojas was not concerned about his availability for the rest of the series and going forward. Rojas probably will not be in the Dodgers' starting lineup for Game 4 of the series on Wednesday at Truist Park against Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle, but it sounds like he should be available off the bench. The 37-year-old Venezuelan infielder has made two starts so far in the NLDS against the Braves and has gone 1-for-4 with a double and a strikeout. He was hitless in three at-bats with a strikeout in Tuesday's Game 3 win before being replaced at second base by Tommy Edman. Rojas has mostly been a bench player for the Dodgers in his 13th year in the league (fourth with L.A.) in 2026, but he proved in last year's World Series that he is still capable of coming through in the clutch when needed. He hit .267 (60-for-225) with four homers and 23 RBI during the regular season.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Fabian Ardaya
Oct 7, 2026, 11:57 AM ET
St. Louis Cardinals right-handed closer Riley O'Brien was a first-time All-Star in 2026 in his first full season as the team's closer, and he ended the year tied with San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller for the National League lead in saves (38) with a 4.08 ERA across a career-high 64 innings pitched. O'Brien also set a career high in appearances (66) in his first full year as a big-leaguer. He did not allow an earned run in his first 13 appearances of the year and ended the first half with a 3.43 ERA and a 7.9% walk rate in 39 1/3 frames. O'Brien had 24 saves in his first 28 opportunities. But in 27 appearances after the All-Star break, O'Brien had a 5.11 ERA in 24 2/3 innings, and his walk rate rose to 14.4% while he went 14-for-18 in save chances. Three of his blown saves in the second half came in September, and five of his losing decisions came in his final 13 outings. The 31-year-old said he experienced "fatigue" in the closing days of the season and that his legs have "been feeling heavy compared to how they felt early in the year," according to Daniel Guerrero of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. As he tired, the velocity of O'Brien's pitches suffered. To be able to maintain velocity through the entire season, O'Brien said he plans to focus on putting on "as much muscle as I can."--Keith Hernandez
Source: St. Louis Post-Dispatch - Daniel Guerrero
Curtis Mead the Favorite to Start at Second Base Next Year


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 11:47 AM ET
Boston Red Sox infielder Curtis Mead is considered the favorite to open next season as the team's starting second baseman, according to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. The Red Sox acquired Mead from the Washington Nationals at the trade deadline this summer, but he ended up playing in only one game for Boston due to a fractured wrist that he suffered in his second at-bat with the team. The 25-year-old will now have all offseason to heal up, and he will enter spring training as the team's primary option at the keystone as they attempt to get back to the playoffs in 2027. The Australian native was having a breakout 2026 campaign with the Nationals before being traded to Boston, and he finished the year with a .253/.353/.498 slash line with an .851 OPS, 17 home runs, 48 RBI, 49 runs scored, and six stolen bases in 285 at-bats in 88 combined games with Washington and Boston. "That would be, I would say, broadly our plan," said manager Chad Tracy when asked about second base. "He was acquired for a reason. You see the numbers that kind of project at least toward a 30-home run season. And adding that, we were really excited about that."--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Boston Globe - Tim Healey
Walker Buehler to Start Game 4 of NLDS Against Brewers


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 11:36 AM ET
The San Diego Padres announced that veteran right-hander Walker Buehler will make the start in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday night at Petco Park against the visiting Milwaukee Brewers. Buehler will make his first postseason appearance this year after going 9-6 with a 4.63 ERA (4.51 FIP) and 1.35 WHIP with 131 strikeouts and 57 walks in 153 2/3 innings pitched across his 32 starts for the Padres in his first season with the team. The 32-year-old is no longer the high-end ace that he was with the Los Angeles Dodgers, but he does have plenty of postseason experience, posting a 3.04 ERA (3.21 FIP) with 114 strikeouts and 36 walks in 94 2/3 innings pitched. Buehler's last start came on Sept. 26 against the division-rival Arizona Diamondbacks, when he allowed four runs (three earned) with a walk and three strikeouts in just 3 2/3 innings for a no-decision. He picked up a win in his only outing against Milwaukee in 2026, giving up just one earned run with two walks and five strikeouts in six innings at Petco Park back on Aug. 11. Buehler will most definitely be on a short leash in a must-win game for San Diego if he is not on his game early on.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Padres PR
Adrian Morejon Dealing With "Stickiness in his Shoulder"


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 11:28 AM ET
San Diego Padres left-handed reliever Adrian Morejon (shoulder) was unavailable in Game 3 of the National League Division Series at Petco Park on Tuesday night against the Milwaukee Brewers due to "stickiness in his shoulder," manager Craig Stammen told AJ Cassavell of MLB.com. There is still a chance that Morejon will be available for Game 4 against the Brewers in San Diego on Wednesday night as the Friars attempt to force a Game 5 back in Milwaukee on Friday night. With Morejon unavailable and closer Mason Miller on the paternity list, the Padres' bullpen was very short on Tuesday night, but Game 1 starter Michael King came to the rescue and threw the final two innings for SD to pick up a save in the 4-3 victory. Morejon has already had two two-inning appearances in this postseason, once in the Wild-Card Series against the Chicago Cubs and again on Saturday against the Brewers in Game of the NLDS, when he allowed the game-winning home run to catcher William Contreras. The hard-throwing Cuban left-hander was one of the most effective late-inning setup men during the regular season, though, going 9-3 with a 2.83 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, three saves, and a career-high 107 strikeouts in just 86 innings out of the bullpen. With Miller unlikely to be back with the team on Wednesday, the Padres could really use Morejon's left arm on Wednesday evening.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - AJ Cassavell
Oct 6, 2026, 10:58 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman was one of the stars of his team's 3-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday. Freeman had just one hit in four plate appearances, but it was a solo home run off Braves ace Chris Sale. Freeman put together another strong regular season in 2026, hitting .288/.362/.430 with 16 home runs, 70 RBI, 74 runs scored, and seven stolen bases. The 37-year-old's production tailed off late in the year, as he hit just .184 in September and slugged just one home run across 249 plate appearances after the All-Star break. However, Freeman has looked like his vintage self so far this postseason. Across the first three games of the NLDS, Freeman has logged four hits, two home runs, two RBI, and three runs scored.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 6, 2026, 10:40 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers utility man Enrique Hernandez struck one of the big blows of his team's 3-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday, clubbing a two-run home run off of Braves ace Chris Sale to open the scoring in the fourth inning. It was Hernandez's only hit of the night, but it helped the Dodgers chase Sale out of the game after just five innings of work. Hernandez missed a large chunk of the regular season with an oblique injury and was not particularly effective when healthy, hitting .222 with four home runs across 96 plate appearances. However, the 35-year-old has a long history as an unlikely postseason hero. Across 332 career plate appearances in the playoffs, Hernandez has now hit .272 with 18 home runs and 44 RBI.--Will Brady

item.dc:creator: Miguel La Torre; ClutchPoints

After a 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday night, the Yankees were swept out of the playoffs, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. did not try to hide how much it stung. "It's very frustrating," Chisholm
item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Jazz Chisholm Jr. reflects on harsh reality NY is facing after ALDS sweep appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees' season ended far sooner than anyone in the Bronx expected. After a 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday night, the Yankees were swept out of the playoffs, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. did not try to hide how much it stung.
"It's very frustrating," Chisholm told reporters after the game. "You can see on my face, you can see on everybody else's face, we're not happy. Nobody wants to go home. Have to go home and think about it for another four months before the season starts up again."
"It's very frustrating. You can see on my face, you can see on everybody else's face we're not happy. Nobody wants to go home. Have to go home and think about it for another 4 months before the season starts up again"
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
– Jazz Chisholm Jr. on the Yankees being swept in the ALDS pic.twitter.com/pA6RGicez1
— SNY Yankees (@snyyankees) October 8, 2026
Those four months will feel even longer given how the series ended. Trailing 4-2 in the sixth inning at Yankee Stadium, Anthony Volpe drove a Griffin Jax fastball toward the left-field wall for what looked like a game-tying two-run homer. Instead, a fan in the first row reached over and touched the ball as Victor Mesa Jr. leaped at the wall.
After a review, umpires ruled spectator interference. Volpe was awarded an RBI double, George Lombard Jr. scored, and the Yankees were left a run short.
Mesa had already done damage in the top half of the inning, taking Max Fried deep for a go-ahead solo homer on the left-hander's final pitch. Fried allowed four runs over 5 2/3 innings.
New York never got the tying run home. Rays closer Bryan Baker walked a batter in the ninth before striking out Trent Grisham to send Tampa Bay to the ALCS for the third time in franchise history.
The series slipped away from the Yankees quickly. Drew Rasmussen carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning of a 1-0 Game 1 win for the Rays. Tampa Bay then took Game 2 by a 5-2 score, capitalizing on four Yankees errors.
The early exit caps a frustrating year for a team that won 93 games but still finished 4 1/2 games behind the Rays in the AL East. It also extends the franchise's World Series drought to 17 seasons, dating back to its 2009 title.
For Chisholm and the rest of the clubhouse, there is nothing left to do but wait. The questions about what went wrong, and what needs to change, will hang over the Yankees all winter.

item.title: [Yardbarker] New York Yankees Make Jarring Jazz Chisholm Announcement
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto
item.description: The New York Yankees have reached the edge of their season with a lineup change that puts Jazz Chisholm Jr. on the bench for Game 3 of the American League Division Series. New York trails the series two games to none and plays Wednesday night with elimination on the line. The move follows a rough n
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have reached the edge of their season with a lineup change that puts Jazz Chisholm Jr. on the bench for Game 3 of the American League Division Series.
Manager Aaron Boone, looking for any spark after a flat offensive stretch against the Tampa Bay Rays, dropped Chisholm from the starting nine and handed second base to Anthony Volpe, via Underdog MLB.
New York trails the series two games to none and plays Wednesday night with elimination on the line.
The move follows a rough night in Game 2. The Yankees lost 5-2 and committed four errors, three of them in the first inning, even with right-hander Cam Schlittler on the mound.
Boone had already hinted that he might shuffle the order in search of life at the plate. Sitting Chisholm is the clearest piece of that shuffle. The infielder had started each of the Yankees’ last three playoff games and gone 2-for-9.
The rest of the card is rearranged as well.
Trent Grisham moves into the leadoff spot in center field. Ben Rice, Luis García Jr. and Cody Bellinger follow him in the order, with Rice serving as the designated hitter, García at first base and Bellinger in left. George Lombard Jr. starts at shortstop, Austin Wells catches, Spencer Jones plays right field, and José Caballero takes third base in place of Ryan McMahon and bats ninth. Max Fried gets the ball.
That order, posted ahead of the game, is a clear attempt to reset an attack that has gone quiet.
After scoring 18 runs across two games against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, New York has managed almost nothing against Tampa Bay.
Outside of two solo home runs by Rice in Game 2, the Yankees have only five hits combined in the series. The Rays have controlled the tempo, and the defensive mistakes in the first inning of Game 2 only widened the gap.
Boone’s decision does not read as a permanent verdict on Chisholm so much as a short-series adjustment. Postseason at-bats are scarce, and a 2-for-9 stretch is enough to cost a starter a night when a team is one loss from going home. V
olpe’s return to the infield also gives Boone a different defensive look at second after the error-filled opener of the series. Caballero’s insertion at third points the same way: cleaner defense, and a different bat at the bottom of the order.
Whether any of it matters will be settled quickly. Fried has to keep the game close, and the top of the order — Grisham, Rice, García and Bellinger — has to produce the contact that has been missing.
If the Yankees fall behind early again, the benching of Chisholm will be remembered as one more adjustment that arrived too late. If they win, it becomes the first step in a series that is still theoretically alive, if only barely.

item.content:encoded:
Despite the impending birth of his firstborn child, Max Fried is starting Game 3 as the Yankees look to avoid elimination from the ALDS.
During his last outing against the Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Fried held steadfast through six innings, striking out six and giving up a home run (a solo shot). With an offense that isn’t offering much support outside of Ben Rice, the Yankees can’t afford any mistakes from Fried tonight as they anticipate continuing their postseason run with a win at home. There’s no doubt that the roars from the Bronx crowd in an elimination game can be intimidating, but Fried must block out the noise to stay focused on shutting down the Rays’ offense.
It’s possible that home-field advantage could help the Yankees’ offense and hopefully fuel some fire as they fight through every at-bat. They’ll need as much ammunition as they can get to face Rays righty Nick Martinez, who has a 2.25 ERA through 12 innings in the Bronx this season with 14 hits and three earned runs allowed.
Yankees skipper Aaron Boone is expected to shuffle around the lineup heading into the do-or-die scenario, and it would be reassuring to give a few guys on the bench, including José Caballero and Anthony Volpe, a shot at making the start. Errors from Game 1 and Game 2 starters Ryan McMahon and Jazz Chisholm Jr. have frustrated fans, to say the least, and it would be reassuring to give Caballero and Volpe a shot at keeping the Yankees’ postseason run going for another day. Boone was reportedly considering starting Volpe at third over McMahon for Game 2, but was quoted as saying he wanted to “prioritize the defense.”
Volpe made his last postseason start in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series and got a hit off Red Sox rookie Payton Tolle. Caballero, on the other hand, has yet to make his postseason debut at the plate this year. He does, however, have decent numbers against righties this season, batting .233 with .295 OBP and .666 OPS.
The Yankees have their work cut out for them as they strive to stay alive against Tampa Bay, and hopefully we’ll see some changes to the starting nine that can instill some feelings of confidence.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will take their home field Wednesday night with their backs against the wall.
The Yanks are facing elimination as they trail the Tampa Bay Rays 2-0 in the American League Division Series, needing three straight wins to move on.
It goes without saying that the Yanks should like their chances to survive at least one more day, as Max Fried will toe the slab in the Bronx - unless the offense continues to have other plans.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
However, rumors swirled that Fried is expecting a baby at any moment, potentially putting his start in jeopardy.
Fried, without getting "too into the personal stuff," confirmed Tuesday the news that he is having a baby "any day now." However, no matter what happens, Fried will be on the bump in the Bronx.
"I've got a really supportive family that understands that this is my job, and it's not going to affect what happens tomorrow," Fried said.
When asked if the baby "complicated" any plans, he simply answered, "No."
Fried's commitment to the Yanks came just hours before the San Diego Padres announced that star closer Mason Miller would miss one to three days after going on the paternity list for the birth of his firstborn. Miller blew a save in Game 2, but his Padres survived without him in Game 3 and trail their series with the Milwaukee Brewers, two games to one.
Fried has missed some time with injuries this season, but when he's been on the mound, he's been his typical ace-like self. He pitched to a 2.80 ERA (35 earned runs/112.2 innings) and is coming off a six-inning, one-run gem against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Round.
The Yankees, however, are hitting .086 this series, and players not named Ben Rice and Austin Wells are a combined 1-for-46.
First pitch in the Bronx is shortly after 8 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
Los Yankees de Nueva York saltarán al campo este miércoles por la noche con la espalda contra la pared.
Los Yankees se enfrentan a la eliminación, ya que van perdiendo por Tampa Bay Rays 2-0 en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, y necesitan tres victorias seguidas para pasar de ronda.
No hace falta decir que a los Yankees les deben parecer bien sus posibilidades de aguantar al menos un día más, ya que Max Fried se subirá al montículo en el Bronx... a menos que la ofensiva siga teniendo otros planes.
Esta página puede contener enlaces de afiliados a socios de apuestas deportivas legales. Si te registras o realizas una apuesta, FOX News podría recibir una compensación. Este contenido lo ha creado un equipo que trabaja de forma independiente de la redacción de FOX News.
Sin embargo, corrían rumores de que Fried está a punto de tener un bebé en cualquier momento, lo que podría poner en peligro su participación como titular.
Fried, sin entrar «demasiado en detalles personales», confirmó el martes la noticia de que va a tener un bebé «en cualquier momento». Sin embargo, pase lo que pase, Fried estará en el montículo en el Bronx.
«Tengo una familia que me apoya muchísimo y que entiende que esto es mi trabajo, y que no va a afectar a lo que pase mañana», dijo Fried.
Cuando le preguntaron si el bebé había «complicado» algún plan, se limitó a responder: «No».
El compromiso de Fried con los Yankees se produjo apenas unas horas antes de que los Padres de San Diego anunciaran que su estrella Mason Miller se perdería entre uno y tres días tras incorporarse a la lista de paternidad por el nacimiento de su primer hijo. Miller falló un salvamento en el segundo partido, pero sus Padres se las arreglaron sin él en el tercero y ahora van perdiendo la serie contra los Brewers de Milwaukee por dos a uno.
Fried se ha perdido algunos partidos por lesiones esta temporada, pero cuando ha estado en el montículo, ha vuelto a ser el as de siempre. Ha registrado una efectividad de 2,80 (35 carreras limpias en 112,2 entradas) y viene de hacer una gran actuación de seis entradas y una sola carrera contra los Boston Red Sox en la ronda de comodines.
Los Yankees, sin embargo, tienen un promedio de bateo de 0,086 en esta serie, y los jugadores que no se llaman Ben Rice ni Austin Wells suman entre todos 1 de 46.
El primer lanzamiento en el Bronx será poco después de las 20:00 h (hora del Este).

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Yankees' Max Fried just helped fuel the paternity leave debate no one asked for
item.dc:creator: Emma Lingan
item.description: There is apparently a paternity leave debate happening in Major League Baseball this postseason. Why? Seriously. Why are we doing this? San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller missed Game 3 of the NLDS against the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday because his wife, Jordan, went into labor with their first child. The Padres placed Miller on MLB's postseason paternity list, which permits a player to be away from his team for between one and three days. The Padres were facing elimination. Miller is their A
item.content:encoded:
There is apparently a paternity leave debate happening in Major League Baseball this postseason.
Why?
Seriously. Why are we doing this?
San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller missed Game 3 of the NLDS against the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday because his wife, Jordan, went into labor with their first child. The Padres placed Miller on MLB's postseason paternity list, which permits a player to be away from his team for between one and three days.
The Padres were facing elimination. Miller is their All-Star closer. His absence unquestionably mattered from a baseball standpoint. It also shouldn't have required a second of explanation.
Then, on the other side of the country, Max Fried unintentionally gave baseball's worst possible discourse more oxygen.
With the New York Yankees facing elimination in Game 3 of the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays, Fried confirmed Tuesday that he plans to make his scheduled start even if his girlfriend goes into labor. She is due to give birth any day, but Fried said he has a supportive family and that the situation would not affect his availability Wednesday. And that's completely fine, too.
If Fried and his partner have discussed the situation and decided that he should pitch, nobody outside their family has any business telling them otherwise. But Fried's decision cannot become some ridiculous masculinity test for Miller — or for the next player who chooses differently.
Fried pitching through the possibility of his child's birth does not make him tougher, more committed or more serious about winning than Miller. Miller stepping away from an elimination game does not mean he cares less about his teammates.
These are deeply personal decisions involving two people, one of whom is quite literally giving birth. They are not clubhouse leadership exercises, and they certainly aren't opportunities for fans to determine which player "wants it more."
Every MLB fan debating paternity leave should remember Alex Vesia
The fact that baseball is having this conversation less than a year after what happened to Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Alex Vesia makes it particularly gross.
Vesia stepped away from Los Angeles before the 2025 World Series because of what the Dodgers initially described only as a "deeply personal family matter." His wife, Kayla, had been expecting their first child.
Later, the Vesias announced that their newborn daughter, Sterling Sol, died on Oct. 26. Vesia missed the World Series because his family needed him during an unimaginable tragedy.
Months later, Vesia explained that leaving his teammates was difficult but the decision itself was easy: his family needed him. That should have ended this conversation forever.
Nobody watching from the couch knows what is happening inside a delivery room. Nobody knows whether a pregnancy that appears routine will remain that way. Nobody knows what complications could arise for the mother or child. Nobody knows what that particular couple has experienced privately before reaching that moment. And frankly, nobody needs to know.
That is exactly why Miller shouldn't have to justify leaving the Padres during an elimination game. It is why Fried shouldn't have to justify pitching for the Yankees, either. The only people whose opinions matter are the players and their partners.
Max Fried, Mason Miller prove there is no ‘right’ way to handle paternity leave
There is also something deeply backward about treating a father being present for childbirth as an optional luxury that becomes increasingly selfish depending on the importance of the baseball game happening that night.
MLB literally has a paternity list for this reason. Miller didn't abandon his teammates. He used a collectively recognized form of leave because his wife was giving birth to their child.
And despite being without their closer, the Padres survived. They beat Milwaukee 4-3, with Michael King recording a six-out save to extend their season. Funny how that works.
Baseball teams are built with 26 players. Organizations have contingency plans for injuries, illness and every other form of unexpected absence because human beings are not machines programmed exclusively around a postseason schedule. Having a baby belongs pretty comfortably in the category of "life event more important than baseball."
Meanwhile, none of this should diminish Fried's choice. The Yankees' season is on the brink, and their ace wants the baseball. Yankees fans can appreciate his willingness to pitch an elimination game while understanding that another player could make the exact opposite decision and deserve precisely the same respect.
That's the distinction this conversation keeps missing. Fried doesn't need to be criticized for pitching, and Miller doesn't need to be criticized for leaving. And after watching the baseball world rally around Vesia and his family less than a year ago, we really shouldn't need another reminder that there are moments when the scoreboard becomes spectacularly insignificant.
A player should never have to wonder whether strangers will accuse him of abandoning his team because he chose to be beside his partner while their child entered the world.
Max Fried has made his choice. Mason Miller made his. Both were theirs to make. There never needed to be a debate in the first place.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Breaking Down One Way Yankees Could Get Aaron Judge on the ALDS Roster

item.description: Max Fried took the sentiment "married to the game" literally when he said he would take the bump in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, whether his girlfriend gave birth or not. The New York Yankees would never push him to make that decision. Still, they're probably secretly happy, seeing as their big-money southpaw has been one of the league's better starters for years, and they signed him after Juan Soto went to Flushing. While it seems a bit uncouth to start thinking strategy when
item.content:encoded:
Max Fried took the sentiment "married to the game" literally when he said he would take the bump in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, whether his girlfriend gave birth or not. The New York Yankees would never push him to make that decision. Still, they're probably secretly happy, seeing as their big-money southpaw has been one of the league's better starters for years, and they signed him after Juan Soto went to Flushing.
While it seems a bit uncouth to start thinking strategy when a man and woman are expecting a baby, the paternity list could be one way for the Yankees to get a start from Fried, and if they win Game 3 on Wednesday night, activate Aaron Judge from the IL on Thursday. Not only is this happening with Fried, but on the West Coast, the Padres saw their star closer, Mason Miller, hit the Postseason Paternity List, and in his stead is former Yankee Wandy Peralta.
As the MLB PR Account on X explained, Miller can be away from the club for a maximum of one to three days. Once he's back, he'll take Peralta's spot.
Fitting Aaron Judge onto the ALDS roster
Again, the Yankees could do this if they take Game 3 — if they feel Judge is healthy enough to play. Fried can make his start and then, if the season is still alive, hit the Paternity List for the rest of the ALDS. At that point, Games 4 and 5 would play over three days anyway, and the Yankees wouldn't need Fried.
However, if the Yankees take this route, there's no doubt it's a desperate move. Judge wasn't healthy enough to start this series, and if he comes in, he probably still isn't. With the season on the line, though, Aaron Boone would probably feel better having Judge with one good leg out there than no Judge.
If this happens, though, the Yankees would be without Luis Garcia Jr. at first base, and Ben Rice wouldn't serve as the designated hitter. The best version of the Yankees would have Judge in right field, but with a bad calf, they may want him at DH and have Rice at first. This would leave a healthy Garcia out for a hobbled Judge.
That said, the Yankees still need to win Game 3 before even considering this, but the paternity list could be one way to pull it off.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

Max Fried’s relationship is in the headlines in early October.
The New York Yankees‘ left-handed pitcher and his long-time companion, Reni Meyer-Whalley, are expecting their first child.
The timing could’ve been better. Fried is slated to start Game 3 of the ALDS on Wednesday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, and it’s a game that would end the Yankees season if they lose.
This is what he said in the lead-up to the game, via MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch:
“I’ve got a really supportive family that that understands that this is my job, and it’s not going to affect what happens tomorrow.”
No matter what the timing ends up being, fans are going to be paying attention to how Fried handles this situation. There definitely has to be a lot on his mind.
Is Max Fried Married?
No, Max Fried is not married.
He’s in a long-term relationship with his girlfriend, Reni Meyer-Whalley.
They became publicly official in 2024, as they took part in MLB All-Star festivities together.
Who is Reni Meyer-Whalley?
Reni Meyer-Whalley is a native of Los Angeles who played Division I volleyball.
Her career began at the University of Washington before she transferred to USC.
Meyer-Whalley was a libero and a defensive specialist, working to stop the other team from scoring — a role Fried holds on the diamond in a different way.
She had actually stepped away from volleyball in the middle of her college tenure before coming back to the court for the Trojans.
“My volleyball journey has been interesting to say the least,” Meyer-Whalley said during her time at USC. “It’s been really long. I’ve been playing since I was 8, and I also never thought that I’d make it here.”
For those volleyball fans out there looking for a few stats: Meyer-Whalley finished her final season at USC with 268 digs, including a season-high of 15 in one match. She also served 29 aces that year.
Meyer-Whalley studied communication and media studies at USC, and her collegiate bio lists her as one of nine children.
Sports Illustrated describes the start of their public-facing relationship like this:
“Exactly when Fried and Meyer-Whalley began dating isn’t publicly known, and the two haven’t offered much help filling in the blanks. Their relationship became public in July 2024, when they attended the MLB All-Star Red Carpet Show together in Arlington, Texas. They walked the carpet holding hands, marking a rare public glimpse into the pitcher’s life away from baseball.”
Now, they’re side by side as Fried navigates what it’s like to pitch in the playoffs for the Yankees, and soon they’ll be welcoming new life into the world together.

item.content:encoded:
NY Daily News | James O'Connell: The Yankees ran out the same exact lineup in Games 1 and 2 of their ALDS matchup against the Rays, but aside from Ben Rice and his pair of home runs no one else is really contributing. As the series shifts over to New York for Game 3 tonight, manager Aaron Boone was amenable to some lineup tinkering though he wouldn't get into specifics of who could find their way in and who would get sent to the bench. Some of the more likely candidates to sit include those who both haven't found their way into a hit yet and also fumbled the ball around in their atrocious Game 2 showing, such as Ryan McMahon and Jazz Chisholm Jr.
NY Post | Mark W. Sanchez: Max Fried is lined up to start tonight on the mound in Game 3, but there was the potential for that to not be the case. Fried's partner is due to give birth in the coming days and there was the possibility that Fried would have to miss this start, but the lefty confirmed that he will be there for the team adding that he's "got a really supportive family that understands that this is my job." Fried's focus is leaving it all on the line for his team as the Yankees face elimination, and hopefully that dedication pays off for him.
MLB.com | Matthew Leach: So the Yankees are down in an 0-2 hole, but is there any hope of a comeback? There's a few reasons to believe in a turnaround, namely that they largely beat themselves in Game 2 and have an elite pitching staff that could lock down opposing bats so long as the defense stops putzing the ball around. Getting out of Tropicana Field is also a big plus, and even though a potential Game 5 would see them return to that house of horrors, they've got to win the first two before worrying about that.
MLB.com | Mike Lupica: The Yankees are certainly not strangers to reverse sweeping in an ALDS, as Lupica takes us through the history of the team's ability to flip the script. Unfortunately, that history all lies in the recent past as Aaron Boone's squads have largely been unable to answer back after getting punched in the face in a series — let's see if they can change that narrative this time around.
The Big Lead | J.P. Hoornstra: Sadly, we end our notes with the passing of 'Sudden' Sam McDowell, who died on Monday. McDowell was a six-time All-Star throughout his 15-year MLB career, and he played for the Yankees at the tail end of his career for the 1973-74 seasons. From all of us here at Pinstripe Alley, we send our condolences to Sam's family and friends.

item.title: [Orange County Register] ALDS: Down 2-0 to Rays, Yankees’ World Series title drought could grow
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press

After making four errors in a dismal Game 2 defeat, New York’s players and staff arrived home about 5 a.m. on Tuesday in a 2-0 American League Division Series deficit for the second straight year, this time against the Tampa Bay Rays. T
item.content:encoded:
By RONALD BLUM AP Baseball Writer
NEW YORK — Max Fried’s words were as sharp as the break on some of his pitches.
“It’s important to have a little bit of pride and to be able to say: ‘That’s not us and we’re going to prove it,’” the New York Yankees pitcher said.
After making four errors in a dismal Game 2 defeat, New York’s players and staff arrived home about 5 a.m. on Tuesday in a 2-0 American League Division Series deficit for the second straight year, this time against the Tampa Bay Rays. The best-of-five matchup resumes Wednesday night (5 p.m. PT, TBS, truTV) in the Bronx with Fried – a former Harvard-Westlake standout – starting for the Yankees and Nick Martinez for the Rays.
With one more loss to Tampa Bay, the World Series title drought for MLB’s winningest franchise would extend to a 17th season – matching the most since Babe Ruth led New York to its first championship in 1923. New York hasn’t advanced past a higher-seeded team in a postseason series since 2020.
“This group has done a really good job all year of bouncing back through a tough game, through some tough moments in the season and handled it all very well. So that’s my expectation this time. It has to be,” said Manager Aaron Boone, who spoke with players individually rather than give a rah-rah speech.
Tampa Bay could party at Yankee Stadium for the second time in two weeks, after clinching the AL East on Sept 22.
Seeking their first World Series title, the Rays are nearing an AL Championship Series against the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland. They haven’t advanced that far since 2020, when they lost in the World Series to the Dodgers.
Martinez used to sit in the Yankee Stadium bleachers when he played college baseball from 2009-11 at Fordham University, located about 5 miles away.
“I imagine it’s going to be an electric crowd with their season on the line,” he said.
Teams taking 2-0 leads in best-of-five postseason series have won 83 of 93 times, according to MLB. The last comeback from an 0-2 deficit was the 2017 Yankees against Cleveland.
“There’s no taking games off,” Rays outfielder Jonny DeLuca said. “Obviously taking the first two has put us in a really good spot, but it’s still the same mindset going forward.”
ERROR ISSUES
Third baseman Ryan McMahon, second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., shortstop George Lombard Jr. and catcher Austin Wells all made errors in Game 3 that led to three unearned runs in New York’s 5-2 loss.
In addition, Lombard didn’t field Chandler Simpson’s two-hopper and right fielder Spencer Jones allowed Jonathan Aranda’s liner – a ball with 65% hit probability – to fall starting the fifth, which sparked a four-run inning.
“It was just one of those things that it all kind of happened back-to-back-to back,” Lombard said.
Throwing errors by McMahon and Chisholm in the first along with a catcher’s interference call against Wells gave the Yankees their first three-error postseason inning.
“It didn’t seem like we really showed up today,” pitcher Cam Schlittler said.
Two years ago, the Yankees had two errors and a mental lapse that led to five unearned runs in a season-ending Game 5 World Series loss to the Dodgers.
Tampa Bay put 31 balls in play, two shy of the high for any team in a postseason game this year. The Rays were just behind Milwaukee for the top regular-season team batting average, .2585 to .2581, and led the American League in on-base percentage.
Simpson is 12th in sprint speed and DeLuca 16th among players with at least 150 competitive runs this year, according to MLB Statcast.
“Just very contact-oriented,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “Just the speed getting down the line, the urgency it forces on the infielders, really good infielders – it forces them to get out of their comfort zone and make a highlight-reel play. Those are tough to make.”
YANKEES’ VANISHING OFFENSE
New York’s players in the third through seventh spots of the batting order went 0 for 33 with 11 strikeouts in the first two games: Luis García Jr., Jones, Lombard, Chisholm and Trent Grisham.
Aaron Judge’s absence has been glaring.
New York was fourth in runs, 13th in batting average and second in OPS through May 31, its last game before the three-time AL MVP went on the injured list due to a fractured rib.
From June 1 through the end of the season, the Yankees were 24th in runs, 29th in batting average and 27th in OPS. Judge returned for seven games from Sept. 8-16, hitting .174 with three RBIs before a calf strain.
“I’m considering a couple things but haven’t settled on anything,” Boone said of possible lineup changes.
FRIED HAS BABY ON THE WAY
Fried’s longtime girlfriend, Reni Meyer-Whalley, is due to give birth any day.
“I’ve got a really supportive family that understands that this is my job, and it’s not going to affect what happens tomorrow,” he said Tuesday.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rays-Yankees ALDS Game 3 FAQ (Wed., 8 p.m. ET, TBS/HBO Max)
item.dc:creator: Adam Berry; Bryan Hoch
item.description: NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night. Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx? It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the R
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night.
Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx?
It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the Rays are still right where they want to be, holding a commanding 2-0 lead in the series with three chances to advance to the AL Championship Series.
“It's amazing, man. It's exactly the way we wanted to start the series,” Rays closer Bryan Baker said. “To be able to play in front of these fans in this building and take a 2-0 series lead was exactly what we wanted, so it feels really good right now.”
Maybe home-field advantage is what the Yankees need after coming up empty against Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in Game 1 and kicking the ball around the infield in a mistake-filled Game 2 defeat. Or maybe it’ll help to send left-hander Max Fried to the mound, knowing how tough he’s been on Tampa Bay throughout his career.
“We've got to get over it,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Game 2. “We've responded all year to difficult times, and we've got to do that again. We've got to get ourselves up off the mat.”
Tampa Bay’s pitching staff held what looked like a red-hot New York lineup to only two runs in the first 18 innings of this series. If the Rays keep that up, they could enjoy another champagne-soaked night in the city that never sleeps.
“I think it's sweet either way. Doesn't matter the clubhouse,” Rays center fielder Jonny DeLuca said. “Obviously, going over there, having the chance to do that would be pretty special.”
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 of the Yankees-Rays Division Series is set for 8 p.m. ET on Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The game will be broadcast on TBS, truTV and HBO Max.
The ALDS will be available in Spanish on UniMas, while Univision’s TUDN Radio will provide Spanish-language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Rays: Nick Martinez, RHP
Key stats: 7-3, 2.38 ERA in 16 road starts this season
After rolling out Rasmussen in Game 1 and Freddy Peralta in Game 2, Martinez was the logical choice for the Rays with the series moving to the Bronx. The veteran right-hander was a reliable presence on the mound for Tampa Bay all season, as he posted a 3.10 ERA over 180 innings while the club went 22-9 in his starts. He was at his best on the road, including two outings in the Bronx. The first-time All-Star held the Yankees to only three runs over 12 innings in their home ballpark.
Yankees: Max Fried, LHP
Key stats: 5-1, 1.81 ERA in 7 career GS vs. Tampa Bay
Fried is coming off a sharp outing against the Red Sox in the decisive Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series, holding Boston to a run on three hits over six innings. Fried walked one and struck out six, his third postseason start since joining the Yankees.
This will be Fried’s third time facing the Rays this season. He last saw them on Sept. 22 in New York, taking the loss in a 6 2/3-inning effort as Tampa Bay clinched the AL East.
Fried also went up against the Rays on April 11 at Tropicana Field, taking a no-decision after permitting three runs over eight innings. For his career, Fried is 5-1 with a 1.81 ERA in seven starts vs. Tampa Bay, including 3-0 with a 0.84 ERA in three starts during the 2025 season.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Rays: It seems likely the Rays will change things up a bit against the Yankees’ left-handers, opting for the right-handed side of most platoons and leaving their lefty hitters available off the bench. Here’s one potential look for a more right-handed lineup.
Yankees: The Yankees have used the same lefty-heavy lineup three times this postseason against right-handed pitchers, including twice in the ALDS. Boone said he is considering shaking things up for Game 3. Boone said before Game 2 that he was considering starting Anthony Volpe at third base. Jose Caballero and Paul Goldschmidt could also enter the mix.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: The Rays really couldn’t be in much better shape thanks to their starting rotation. Rasmussen handled eight innings in Game 1, and the duo of Peralta and Ian Seymour combined to work 7 2/3 innings in Game 2. So, their traditional relievers have recorded seven of the 54 outs so far this series: six from Baker and a big one from lefty Cam Booser. They may not turn to Peralta or Seymour in Game 3, but they still have starter Griffin Jax available -- and the Yankees have yet to face setup men Tyler Wells and Kevin Kelly in this series.
Yankees: Ryan Weathers replaced infielder/outfielder Amed Rosario for this series, returning from a left flexor strain sustained in late August. David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick should all be leaned upon for high-leverage outs. Will Warren is now in the bullpen after appearing in 32 games (29 starts) during the regular season. Warren made one appearance in the Wild Card Series, tossing 1 2/3 innings.
Any injuries of note?
Rays: Nothing new. Everyone who was expected to be available for this series is on the roster. The most notable injury situation to watch moving forward is that of left-hander Shane McClanahan, whose status is unclear except that he will not pitch in this series.
Yankees: Aaron Judge was left off the ALDS roster, though Boone said it was a “close” call. Judge has yet to run the bases as he recovers from a right calf strain, though he has been performing outfield running. He has also been taking numerous live at-bats while throwing. Clarke Schmidt has been ruled out for the remainder of the postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Aranda doesn’t get as much love as the other members of the “Big Three,” but his left-handed bat is key. He hit better than either Caminero or Díaz in September, and he had the lone big hit of the night in Game 1 before picking up two more hits in Game 2. Richie Palacios finished strong, too, posting a .981 OPS with five homers in September before delivering the biggest hit of Game 2, and the Brooklyn native likes hitting against his hometown Yankees. Tampa Bay’s entire rotation surged into the postseason, highlighted by Rasmussen and Peralta, the September AL Pitcher of the Month.
The Rays’ outfield is off to a slow start in this series, offensively, but they all showed the impact they can have by putting the ball in play in Game 2. And their defense has been consistently excellent.
Yankees: Rice has been the Yankees' most productive hitter in the postseason, and given how the ALDS has gone, it hasn't been particularly close. Rice is 7-for-15 (.467) in the playoffs, including his two-homer performance in ALDS Game 2. Rice has four homers and eight RBIs overall. Wells is 5-for-12 (.417) in the playoffs, including a couple of doubles in the ALDS. Everyone except for Rice and Wells has combined to go 1-for-46 (.022) in the ALDS so far.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Yankees won four of the six games these clubs played in the Bronx during the regular season, splitting a pair of games in late May, then taking three of four the final week of the season. However, the Rays have already celebrated once at Yankee Stadium, as they clinched the AL East title with a 6-1 win in the second half of a doubleheader on Sept. 22.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Yankees' Max Fried Reveals ALDS Game 3 Plans With Baby On Way
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: There will be those who agree wholeheartedly with Max Fried’s thinking, and there will be those who disagree entirely. That won’t change Fried’s decision, though. The New York Yankees‘ left-handed pitcher is slated to start Game 3 of the ALDS on Wednesday, and that start will come with the potential for a baby to be born to him and his girlfriend any day now. Fried’s girlfriend, the former Division I volleyball player Reni Meyer-Whalley, is just about due. It’s certainly not ideal timing, given
item.content:encoded:
There will be those who agree wholeheartedly with Max Fried’s thinking, and there will be those who disagree entirely.
That won’t change Fried’s decision, though. The New York Yankees‘ left-handed pitcher is slated to start Game 3 of the ALDS on Wednesday, and that start will come with the potential for a baby to be born to him and his girlfriend any day now.
Fried’s girlfriend, the former Division I volleyball player Reni Meyer-Whalley, is just about due.
It’s certainly not ideal timing, given that the Yankees’ season will end if they lose on Wednesday.
On the flip side, this will be the first child for Fried and his significant other.
One way or the other, Fried has to make a potentially tough call.
Max Fried Decision
Fried told reporters on Tuesday afternoon that he will be starting ALDS Game 3 and that he doesn’t expect that plan to change.
This is what he said, via MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch:
“I’ve got a really supportive family that that understands that this is my job, and it’s not going to affect what happens tomorrow.”
Ballplayers through the years have taken all kinds of different approaches to an upcoming baby’s birth, from pulling a player in the middle of a game to letting him get away in advance to be there.
The tricky part about baseball season is that games are almost every day, so if a baby is coming, it’ll likely arrive on a gameday one way or another.
MLB even has a paternity list to allow roster construction to be handled while a new father steps away from the team.
Rarely, though, does this come up in October. It’s pivotal timing, and it’s two big parts of life overlapping for Fried.
Max Fried Sets Up Jokes
Fried’s choice to not miss his start has set up a similar brand of jokes on social media.
This is what one commenter wrote:
“Another egregious error by a yankees player. Your kid being born is once-in-a-lifetime moment. The Yankees getting eliminated in the postseason in embarrassing fashion is an October tradition.”
Then there was this one:
“This man’s about to risk relationship trouble for a team that’s not gonna give him an ounce of run support.”
There’s certainly ample opportunity for Yankees haters to pile on here.
Fried could also have everything work out. There’s no guarantee his child will be born while he pitches on Wednesday night.
It’s not a call that many would like to have to make, though. Fried and the Yankees are in a tough spot, and the team can’t really make a choice of their own here. It’s gotta be up to the pitcher/father.
And right now, it looks like Fried has made up his mind.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Stephen A. Smith Calls Out Yankees Manager Aaron Boone After ALDS Loss

New York sent ace Cam Schlittler to the mound, and while he didn't have his best stuff, the defense behind him didn't help him one bit.
