As a team, they recorded just four hits, following a one-hit performance in Game 1 that
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees fell into an 0-2 hole Monday night after losing to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the ALDS.
New York sent ace Cam Schlittler to the mound, and while he didn't have his best stuff, the defense behind him didn't help him one bit.
The Yankees committed three errors in the first inning and four total for the game as they lost 5-2, with both of their runs coming on solo home runs by Ben Rice. As a team, they recorded just four hits, following a one-hit performance in Game 1 that resulted in a 1-0 loss.
Stephen A. Smith Calls Out Aaron Boone
Now, with the Yankees' backs against the wall and one loss away from elimination, conversations are beginning about what manager Aaron Boone's future looks like in the Bronx.
On Tuesday, ESPN's Stephen A. Smith made it very clear that he's out on Boone after supporting him since he was hired back in 2017 by New York.
"This is a disgrace. I'm looking at Aaron Boone now. I've been a supporter of Aaron Boone for years. I can't support him any longer. You can't have a team out there looking like the bad news bears," Smith said. "It's bad enough that only Ben Rice is hitting the damn ball… but you can't have a professional baseball team in Major League Baseball looking like this. This is disgraceful.
"It ain't one person, it ain't two people, it ain't three people, five different people made errors… I couldn't believe it."
Looking at the Yankees
The ALDS will now shift to New York, where the Yankees will play Game 3 on Wednesday in the Bronx and potentially Game 4 if they can win tomorrow and extend the series.
If they lose one more game, though, the series will conclude, and the Rays will advance to the ALCS, where they'll face the winner of the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians series. The White Sox currently lead that series 2-0.
New York is expected to send left-hander Max Fried to the mound for Game 3, while left-hander Carlos Rodón would start a potential Game 4.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Stephen A. Smith Calls Out Yankees Manager Aaron Boone After ALDS Loss appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] Yankees At-Bat of the Week: George Lombard Jr. (9/30)
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: Welp, the Yankees forgot to bring their bats to Game 1 against the Rays and now they forgot their gloves in Game 2. Five errors in the first five innings destroyed any advantage they might have gained from Cam Schlittler starting, their self-immolation eerily reminiscent of the fifth inning collapse in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series. In an attempt to cling on to a positive memory of these playoffs, I present our first At-Bat of the Week of the 2026 postseason, this edition featuring George Lomb
item.content:encoded:
Welp, the Yankees forgot to bring their bats to Game 1 against the Rays and now they forgot their gloves in Game 2. Five errors in the first five innings destroyed any advantage they might have gained from Cam Schlittler starting, their self-immolation eerily reminiscent of the fifth inning collapse in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series. In an attempt to cling on to a positive memory of these playoffs, I present our first At-Bat of the Week of the 2026 postseason, this edition featuring George Lombard Jr. in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
We join Lombard with no outs in the sixth inning last Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The Yankees blew Boston’s doors off in Game 1, 9-0, on the back of Ben Rice’s historic two home run, six-RBI performance. That game was close until the Yankees blew things open in the eighth, and this game is following a similar pattern with Max Fried and Sonny Gray largely holding both offenses in check.
And just like in Game 1, Chad Tracy came out with a quick hook for his starter, which is how we see Garrett Crochet pitching out of the bullpen to open the sixth. Crochet hadn’t thrown an MLB pitch since April, missing most of the season with a left shoulder injury, but made it back just in time to sneak onto the Wild Card roster. Spencer Jones stands on first after reaching on a leadoff strikeout wild pitch, and as we’ll soon see his hustle down the line will prove to be the turning point in the game.
I can almost guarantee that Lombard and everyone else in the stadium is expecting Crochet’s first MLB pitch in over five months to be his overpowering four-seamer. Perhaps Crochet looks to play off this expectation, because he introduces a wrinkle with a first pitch cutter trying to get a hitter sitting four-seamer to chase below the zone.
The intent is sound but the execution isn’t quite there. This pitch starts as a ball low out of Crochet’s hand and never looks like a strike. Lombard isn’t tempted to chase and spits on this cutter for ball one.
After showing Lombard a fastball that breaks glove-side, there is an opportunity for Crochet to steal a called strike inside. His four-seamer breaks in the opposite direction as the cutter, so a pitch that starts a little in off the plate and tails back to the inside edge should freeze the hitter.
It’s clear Crochet’s command is rusty given he misses his target on the opposite side of the plate. He wants to get this four-seamer in under Lombard’s hands but instead lands it low and away, just out of the zone. It still requires an impressively disciplined take from Lombard given it lands mere inches from the outside edge, made doubly difficult considering it immediately follows a cutter that breaks toward the plate from outside to in.
Lombard has worked the count leverage in his favor, 2-0. You’d expect most pitchers to come into the zone with a heater to avoid falling behind, 3-0, especially a pitcher with as blazing a fastball as Crochet’s.
Lombard completely sells out for the four-seamer and is made to look a little bit foolish on this back foot cutter. Make no mistake, this is a filthy pitch from Crochet. It looks like a strike middle-down out of the hand before the late movement zips it down and in under Lombard’s bat.
So far, the cutter appears to be coming out of Crochet’s hand a lot better than the four-seamer. After getting the chase and whiff on the previous one, he doubles up with another back foot cutter.
Crochet is able to pinpoint the bottom rail of the zone with this cutter for called strike two. Lombard is taking all the way to give Jones the opportunity to steal second . It’s a good thing he didn’t swing, because an errant throw to second from Adley Rutschman allows Jones to take the extra base, putting him 90 feet away from scoring an invaluable insurance run. Even if Jones hadn’t been running on the play, I still like this take from Lombard — this pitch had tailor-made groundball written all over it.
In the span of two pitches, Crochet has swung the count leverage in his favor, from 2-0 to 2-2. Having shown Lombard three cutters out of four pitches and with his first chance for a strikeout, Crochet attempts to gas a four-seamer by the Yankees rookie, the pitch coming in seven mph faster and with eleven inches less drop than the cutter.
What a swing by Lombard! This is a nasty heater from Crochet, 98 mph and just off the corner up and away. The situational hitting by Lombard is mature well beyond his 21 years. Living by the old adage of hitting the ball back the way it came, Lombard stays through this outside heater and shoots it to the opposite field for an RBI single. It’s such a simple approach and swing — short and compact to the pitch making sure to stay behind the baseball — the rookie not trying to do anything more than the pitch will allow him to do, knowing that solid contact the other way is almost certain to get the run in.
Here’s the full AB:
Proper credit has to be awarded to Jones as the precursor to this AB. Not giving up on the play when he struck out, the wheels to steal second and then the awareness to see the ball rolling into center and take off for third put Crochet on the ropes, and Lombard’s single opened the floodgates. To get that kind of mature contribution from a pair of your homegrown rookies in the playoffs against your age old rival is such a shot in the arm for the rest of the team. And returning to Lombard, I cannot say enough about how mature his approach was in this AB. It would be easy for any player, especially a 21-year-old rookie in his first postseason, to let the tension and stress creep in after Crochet quickly flipped the count from 2-0 to 2-2. However, he clutched up and came through with one of the finer pieces of situational hitting you are likely to see this postseason, giving his team an indispensable two-run cushion and setting the stage for the fireworks that would follow later in the frame.

Ahora, los Yanquis regresan a casa con la obligación de cambiar la historia. El tercer partido de la serie se disputará m
item.content:encoded:
- martes 06 de octubre de 2026 - 11:00 AM
Los Yanquis de Nueva York están contra las cuerdas y necesitan reaccionar de inmediato si quieren mantener con vida su camino en los playoffs de las Grandes Ligas.
Nueva York cayó anoche 5-2 ante los Rays de Tampa Bay en el Tropicana Field anoche y quedó abajo 2-0 en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, a punto de ser eliminados.
Ahora, los Yanquis regresan a casa con la obligación de cambiar la historia. El tercer partido de la serie se disputará mañana en el Yankee Stadium, desde las 7:00 de la noche, donde Nueva York buscará aprovechar el respaldo de su afición para iniciar la remontada.
Para este encuentro, los Yanquis enviarán al montículo al zurdo Max Fried, mientras que Tampa Bay contará con el derecho Nick Martínez.
El margen de error es mínimo para los neoyorquinos. Una derrota significa el final de la temporada.
Caballero, con poco juego
El panameño José Caballero volvió a formar parte del equipo durante el segundo encuentro, aunque su participación estuvo limitada a labores defensivas.
Caballero ingresó para jugar la tercera base, en el octavo episodio, pero no tuvo turnos oficiales al bate durante el partido.
El santeño ha sido poco utilizado por los Yanquis en esta ronda, a pesar de su velocidad y defensa.
El Yankee Stadium será ahora el escenario donde Nueva York intentará evitar la eliminación y comenzar una remontada que, hasta el momento, parece cuesta arriba.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are a loss away from watching their season end. The Tampa Bay Rays hold a 2-0 lead in the American League Division Series after back-to-back wins at Tropicana Field. Drew Rasmussen shut them out in Game 1. Four errors helped bury them in Game 2.
The series shifts to Yankee Stadium on Wednesday for Game 3, and the Yankees need a lifeline.
The Yankees May Have a Lifeline
Max Fried will start Game 3 on six days of rest.
The left-hander is 3-1 against Tampa Bay across five starts since signing with New York.
His most recent outing for the Yankees came in the Wild Card round, when he held the Red Sox to one run across six innings in Game 2. That performance came on the same mound he will pitch on Wednesday.
Fried posted a 2.80 ERA across 112 2/3 innings during the regular season while missing time with a left elbow bone bruise. His 104 strikeouts were modest by ace standards, but strikeouts have never been the foundation of what makes him effective.
What the Matchup Looks Like on Paper
The Rays posted the lowest strikeout rate in baseball this season at 18.8 percent. They put the ball in play constantly and create pressure with speed and situational contact.
Opposing hitters barreled just 2.4 percent of the balls they put in play against Fried this season, and his groundball numbers ranked among the best in the league. Tampa Bay's offense also performed worse against left-handed pitching throughout the regular season.
Final Word for the Yankees
The numbers suggest the matchup bodes well for Fried. That does not guarantee anything. The Yankees defense still has to hold up behind him, and the offense still has to score.
Wednesday will tell the rest.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees Have Reason for Optimism Ahead of Must-Win Rays Game appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
I hate Tropicana Field. I know many of you do too. If you are not a Yankees fan and are doing what I am also guilty of doing—reading the reactions of salty fans after playoff losses—grab your popcorn. This is the good stuff you’re probably looking for.
It blows my mind that baseball games in 2026 are played at places like this. It honestly blows my mind even more that this place was destroyed by an act of God two years ago, was rebuilt despite plans to replace it in the near future, and is being used for big playoff games. The roof is baseball-colored; there is statistical proof that teams other than the Rays struggle defensively here due to a lack of experience; the turf leads to weird hops that cause more errors to be committed against Tampa Bay than any other team in baseball. It’s the strangest home-field advantage in baseball, and one that the Rays ran roughshod over to take advantage of a Yankees team that was just not focused from the jump tonight—and one that, to be clear, absolutely deserved this atrocious loss, even if it was played in the baseball version of Elysian Fields.
Alright, enough of my anger-filled soapbox. The Yanks set the tone for this one with three brutal first-inning errors, played shoddy defense the rest of the night, and just got Rays’d. Any opportunity they had to use their speed or slap hitting, they used it. The Yankees were not prepared. Aside from two home runs from Ben Rice and an oh-so-close deep fly out from Cody Bellinger with the bases juiced, the offense was dead again in a 5-2 loss that puts the season on the brink.
When you get no-hit for nearly eight innings the game before, you desperately want to get the monkey off your back early the next night. The quality of contact was good in that first inning against Freddy Peralta, with a warning-track fly out from Rice and a scorched Bellinger lineout, but the Yankees went quietly in the first before the utter chaos of the bottom half.
On just Cam Schlittler’s second pitch of the game, Yandy Díaz hit a soft Trop chopper to Ryan McMahon, which he promptly booted after misreading the hop. Jonathan Aranda then lined a single up the middle for the one real hit in the inning. Needing a double play, Schlittler got Junior Caminero to spike a ball into the turf that was snared by George Lombard Jr. for a brilliant flip for a forceout. Unfortunately, Jazz Chisholm Jr. decided to throw the ball into the dugout with no chance to turn two, giving the Rays the early lead.
The defensive inning from hell continued when a three-pitch strikeout from Liam Hicks was overturned into a catcher’s interference error on Austin Wells. Awarding a batter a base for a check-swing catcher’s interference is dumb, and I will forever believe that. The speedy Chandler Simpson ripped a ball to second for what looked like a tailor-made double play, but an awful throw from Chisholm pulled Lombard off the bag. The rookie shortstop somehow managed to tap the bag after to avoid a fourth error in the inning, and Cam survived the inning from hell with only one run allowed.
We got more Trop shenanigans when Spencer Jones hit a ball a mile high off the B-ring in center field, which was caught by Victor Mesa Jr. Objectively, almost every other team drops that ball because of their lack of experience reading fly balls here, but the Rays caught it, naturally. Two more quick outs had Peralta rolling through two.
Jonny DeLuca golfed an 0-2 curveball in the dirt for a leadoff double in the second, but was stranded on a trio of groundouts surrounding a two-out walk. The bottom of the order went down quietly as well, giving Peralta a perfect game through three innings just one night after Rasmussen’s brilliance. At this point, I’m not sure the vibes could get much worse.
Schlittler continued to grind through the third, allowing singles to Caminero and Simpson, but got out of a jam after a 108.5 mph scorched grounder from DeLuca was fielded cleanly by Lombard to end the threat. Just one batter later, with the Yankees entering their 13th inning of the series with just one hit, Rice allowed everyone on the team and in the fanbase to breathe for a second, smashing a leadoff home run in the fourth to tie the game at one.
Bellinger followed with a single, but was stranded by the next three hitters. Schlittler responded to the desperate gasp for a shutdown inning, retiring the Rays in order with help from a surprisingly solid play by Trent Grisham in center field. Peralta seemed to be cruising again after retiring the first two in the fifth, but things got interesting after a bullet double by Austin Wells and a gritty walk by Ryan McMahon. The ever-aggressive Kevin Cash pulled him for Cam Booser, betting on his lefty specialist to neutralize the best hitters on the team.
He walked Rice on five pitches to bring up Bellinger with the bases loaded. This was the moment. This was where the Yankees could show who they were. For a brief second, it seemed like they would. The All-Star left fielder absolutely pummeled a bad 0-2 fastball to deep center field. 102.9 mph, 405 feet. In 12 ballparks, it’s a grand slam. In some others, it’s off the wall. Unfortunately, as has happened all too many times in the postseason in the Judge era, the big hit fell just a few inches short, landing harmlessly in the glove of DeLuca.
It’s the type of gut punch that takes the air out of a fan, and maybe it took the air out of the team. It’s not how baseball works, but maybe it is. Schlittler allowed a bullet single (that Jones maybe should’ve caught?) and a bullet double from Caminero to set up second and third with nobody out. Usually, a team’s cleanup and five-hole hitters wouldn’t be conducive to 55 and 65 mph choppers that bounce two feet in front of home plate in RBI opportunities, but these are the Rays. Both runs scored on back-to-back Baltimore chops that the Yankees had no chance of getting an out at the plate on, even if Lombard had defended the latter cleanly. That gave the Rays a 3-1 lead.
The frustration didn’t end there. After Brent Headrick entered and struck out Mesa, we got another Trop chop grounder to Lombard. Due to the bounce the ball took and the speed of DeLuca, he had to rush the throw, which forced a long stretch from Luis García Jr. If the play was made cleanly, DeLuca would’ve been out by an eyelash, which tells you how perfect they had to be, but García couldn’t squeeze the throw, and everyone was safe. Another error. One batter later, Richie Palacios hit a two-run single to effectively ice this one, making it 5-1 Rays.
We then hit a weird point in the game. Ian Seymour came in for the Rays as a lefty bulk reliever, but Aaron Boone elected to keep his righties in the dugout. As a fan who was resigned to the outcome after the Palacios single, it seems like nothing, but damn, that’s pretty rough of your manager to be so apathetic in this spot. The lineup had no pulse against him in some rough matchups.
Playing out the string, John Schreiber tossed a scoreless sixth, Ryan Weathers and Paul Blackburn combined for the seventh, and Blackburn and David Bednar combined for the ninth. For the offense, all they had left was another home run for Rice, who continues to have a postseason to remember while his teammates give him no help, like 2018 LeBron.
Bryan Baker got the save in the ninth, 1-2-3, to solidify Game 2 for the Rays. If the Yankees want to win this series and get to the ALCS, they must win three straight against a team they’ve struggled against all year and win a game at Tropicana Field on Saturday after going 2-7 there to start this season. We’re essentially right back where we were a year ago with the Yankees down 0-2 and leaving Toronto. Bleak, I know.
There will be baseball played on Wednesday. After that, it’s up to the Yankees to decide. Game 3 will be at Yankee Stadium at 8 pm EDT. It’s Max Fried (pending the birth of his child) against a pitcher to be determined, but it will likely be Nick Martinez.

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Boone is sure Cam Schlittler is built for moments like getting the start against the Rays in the ALDS.
During his conversation with the media ahead of Game 2 on Monday, the Yankees’ skipper responded to comments about Schlittler’s confidence when the lights are brightest. The Division Series was a bit bumpier for him in 2025 than the Wild Card Series showdown with Boston, so he’ll look to put that behind him. The 25-year-old righty will be making his second career ALDS start and will look to continue his current postseason hot streak as New York faces Tampa Bay.
“You never know a result is going to be in a given game, but he’s certainly equipped to handle it,” Boone stated. “He’s got a ton of confidence and is fearless in these spots.”
During his previous postseason outing, Schlittler barred the Red Sox offense from gaining an edge in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, throwing six and a third scoreless innings and racking up 10 strikeouts. It’s no surprise that he showed up and shelled out, following the discourse behind his rivalry with New England fans and media outlets.
The Yankees will have the opportunity to head back to the Bronx, with hopes of a split series, and have Max Fried take the mound for the Game 3 start against Tampa Bay. Boone also announced that Carlos Rodón would get the nod in a possible Game 4 at Yankee Stadium, which New York would very much like to force tonight rather than waiting until Wednesday.
You won’t want to miss a second of Schlittler’s outing as the Yankees face off against the Rays in Game 2 of the Division Series Monday at 8 p.m. EST.

item.content:encoded:
For the second time in three years, we have a shot at seeing the New York Yankees and Los Angeles Dodgers battle it out in the World Series. Both teams continue the postseason this weekend, with the Yankees facing the Rays in the ALDS and the Dodgers welcoming the Braves for an NLDS clash.
Only seven wins separate those four teams — and the other four still alive — from the pennant, and the Yankees looked sharp in their Wild Card Series sweep of the rival Red Sox. Even with Aaron Judge still on the mend, the 27-time World Series champions are built to capture only their third pennant since the start of 2004.
And while casual fans may think Shohei and the Dodgers are guaranteed a third consecutive title, don’t rule out the Yankees just yet.
Welcome to the Yankees’ George Lombard Jr. experience
Somewhere out there is a baseball fan feeling old because they’re watching George Lombard Sr.’s son play for the Yankees. If it’s any consolation, the 2023 first-round pick began his playoff career with four hits — three coming in Game 1 — and three runs scored against the Red Sox. Yep, he belongs, and he clearly can handle the New York spotlight.
Although Lombard’s defensive issues were a significant talking point down the stretch, he handled all seven chances without an error. He also became the youngest Yankees shortstop to start a playoff game at 21 years and 119 days old.
“It’s really cool,” Lombard said following the Wild Card Round. “There’s been a lot of countless legends that have come and played in the pinstripes so it’s really cool.”
How can you complain when you have Cam Schlittler and Max Fried?
No, we’re not forgetting Carlos Rodón or Gerrit Cole, the latter of whom is expected to start Game 1. But Schlittler showed why he’s the presumptive AL Cy Young winner by dominating the Red Sox yet again, allowing only two runs and one walk over 20.2 career postseason innings.
Elbow injuries limited Fried to 20 starts, though his 2.80 ERA and 24.0 percent strikeout rate were both in line with last year’s 2.86 ERA and 23.6 percent strikeout marks. Schlittler is expected to start Game 2, with Fried, Rodón, or Cole likely to follow in Game 3 (depending on who starts the ALDS opener).
The Jazz Chisholm and Austin Wells comeback trains are back on
Wednesday’s Game 2 showed exactly why Chisholm, who reached base three times and recorded two steals, could still command a multi-year deal this offseason. Injuries and a sharp reduction in power make it easy to forget how electrifying the two-time All-Star second baseman is, both as a player and an energetic personality. He marches to the beat of his own drum, and the Yankees need that balance of power, speed, and enthusiasm.
As for Wells, look who finally won back Yankees fans’ support. The embattled catcher quietly hit .229 with a .787 OPS in the second half, drastically up from his .155 and .504 marks over his first 66 games. Any concerns about that being a flash in the pan ended — or at least temporarily paused — after the fourth-year backstop went 3-for-6 with four RBIs in the Wild Card Series.
Imagine telling someone immediately following the trade deadline that Wells and Chisholm are among the Yankees’ most intimidating bats entering the ALDS.
We don’t talk enough about David Bednar and the Yankees’ bullpen
Not only did the Yankees bullpen’s 3.13 ERA lead baseball, but it ranked considerably above the second-place Brewers’ 3.22 mark. Bednar was fantastic in his first full Yankees season, racking up 35 saves — the most by a Yankees closer since Arolis Chapman’s 37 in 2019 — and a 2.47 ERA in 69.1 innings. He’s a pending free agent who has set himself up to cash in, and we’ll see whether the Yankees pay up.
Keep your eyes on Paul Blackburn, who pitched to a career-best 1.69 ERA — nearly three full runs fewer than his lifetime 4.46 ERA — in 85 innings. Although his 9.8 percent walk rate is concerning, he’s carved out a Luke Weaver-type role as a reliable swingman.

item.title: [Newsday] Was Yankees' Gerrit Cole's postseason resume the difference in deciding the ALDS Game 1 starter?

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — One measure of just how good the Yankees' rotation has been this season (and now two games into the postseason) is this oddity:
By choosing to go with Gerrit Cole in American League Division Series Game 1 against the Rays on Saturday night, the Yankees actually left themselves open to second-guessing.
Not all that much, but some.
It was not a surprising announcement and one, considering Cole’s resume, that was somewhat expected.
It was one thing to tell Cole, the ace of pretty much every rotation he’s been a part of, that Cam Schlittler would start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
Schlittler, the presumed American League Cy Young Award winner after going 14-6 with a league-low 1.95 ERA, had one of the best seasons any Yankees pitcher has ever had.
Cole himself would have tabbed Schlittler to start Game 1 against the Red Sox (the Yankees did debate starting Max Fried in Game 1 against Boston but ultimately chose not to outthink themselves and went with the no-brainer decision to start Schlittler).
But telling Cole, who is 11-6 with a 2.77 ERA in 22 career postseason starts — including getting the nod in eight Game 1s — that he would be bypassed for this one even in favor of the red-hot-down-the-stretch Carlos Rodon, might have been dicey.
Based on late-season accomplishment, Rodon certainly belonged in the discussion. As manager Aaron Boone put it Friday before his team worked out at Tropicana Field, Rodon wasn’t merely in play for ALDS Game 1.
“Carlos has been a consideration, literally, [for] Game 1 of the Wild Card, 2 of the Wild Card, potentially Game 3, and every game moving forward,” said Boone, who added that Rodon will start either Game 3 or 4 of this series. “So it's one of those difficult decisions we have, one of those good difficult decisions we have, because we have four guys that are very high-end. So it's at least a conversation every time.”
Rodon put himself in the conversation with his work during the last month-plus. The lefthander, who had two separate stints on the injured list, went 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA in 16 starts and was particularly good late, pitching better than anyone in the rotation not named Schlittler with a 3-1 record and a 1.89 ERA in his final seven starts.
Cole, meanwhile, wasn’t nearly as good as the season drew to a close. He went 10-9 with a 3.61 ERA in 22 starts after beginning the year on the IL while recovering from Tommy John surgery, but in his last seven starts, he went 4-3 with a 4.46 ERA, allowing 11 homers in 40 1/3 innings. He allowed seven home runs in a span of 9 1⁄3 innings against the Padres and Mets and then gave up another one against the Diamondbacks, making it eight in a 13-inning span.
Looking at each pitcher’s last start of the season against the Rays also boosted Rodon’s candidacy for Game 1 of this series.
Facing the Rays on Sept. 22 in the first game of a doubleheader with the Yankees still mathematically alive for the AL East title, Rodon produced perhaps his best outing of the season in a 2-0 victory, allowing three hits in a season-high eight innings.
“One of the best-pitched games I saw all year,” one rival scout said that day.
Facing the Rays in a game without meaning a day later — Tampa Bay had clinched the division title by winning the second game of the Sept. 22 doubleheader — Cole allowed two runs and three hits, including a home run, in 5 2/3 innings of a 9-2 victory. He walked three and struck out eight.
“I thought Carlos really, really pitched well down the stretch,” Cole said on Friday.
But the Yankees weighed more than the stretch run.
The pitchers’ respective postseason resumes don’t compare, for one. Cole has been good far more often than not in his 22 starts, 12 of those with the Yankees, for whom he’s gone 5-2 with a 2.93 ERA. Rodon has been the opposite, 1-3 with a 7.53 ERA in eight games (six of those with the Yankees, going 1-2 with a 6.92 ERA).
Part of the calculus has been Cole’s relative consistency over the years against the Rays and, more significant, at Tropicana Field, where the Rays tied for MLB’s best home record at 55-26 this season.
Cole is 2-4 with a career 3.32 ERA in 10 starts at the Trop and 2-2, 3.52 in six starts as a Yankee in this quirky ballpark. Rodon hasn’t been bad in three career Tropicana Field outings, 0-1 with a 3.68 ERA, but doesn't have nearly the track record there that Cole has.
Cole didn’t throw especially well in this stadium in his one start there this season on July 8, allowing three runs and seven hits in 6 1/3 innings of a 3-0 loss.
Still, as Boone said: “I feel like he's always thrown the ball really well here. Not that that's everything.”
Though not the lone factor in swaying the Yankees, it clearly was far from an insignificant one.

item.content:encoded:
Why Cam Schlittler's 8-word truth bomb will have Yankees fans feeling confident for Rays series appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Is this finally the year the New York Yankees get it together? For years, the Bronx has seen their baseball team make it to the postseason, only to falter in the biggest moments. This year, New York is once again one of the top teams left, despite being a Wild Card team.
The Yankees are up against a truly formidable foe in the first-seeded Tampa Bay Rays. There's a lot of concern about whether this veteran team can go toe-to-toe with their resurgent division rivals. However, ace Cam Schlittler isn't worried about his team in the slightest. Why? Well, here's what the star has to say.
"We're on a roll at the right time," Schlittler said, per Gary Phillips.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Aaron Boone further expanded on that point, saying, "I like the balance of our club right now. Again, we played great baseball in a lot of ways here, obviously anchored by our two great starters that got us off on a great foot. But a lot of really good things happened with this group. We get a chance to keep it going."
The Yankees are coming off a comfortable dismantling of the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round. Schlitter got the start in Game 1, and the ace pitcher immediately showed why he's earned his spot as the postseason opening starter. Schlittler pitches 6 1/3 innings of no-run ball, allowing just two hits while striking out ten batters. The Yankees bullpen finished the job, holding Boston scoreless as their hitting unit scored nine runs.
Max Fried got the ball in Game 2, and he was also incredible for New York. In six innings, the Yankees star allowed just one hit while striking out six. New York cruised to a comfortable 9-2 win to secure their spot in the Wild Card round. They now look to keep that momentum against a well-rested Rays team.

item.content:encoded:
Through all the hand-wringing over the lineup and injury status of Aaron Judge all season, the fact of the matter was that the New York Yankees possess an embarrassment of riches in their starting rotation. It ultimately might be what delivers them another World Series.
So the fact that the Yankees could turn to arguably their fourth-best starting pitcher for Game 1 of their American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays, and only prompt minor debate among observers about the move, is another sign of how stacked the team is on the mound.
Gerrit Cole will start Game 1, the Yankees announced Friday morning, going with the safe choice to open the series. The Rays will counter with All-Star right-hander Drew Rasmussen.
Cole comes into Saturday's game with plenty of rest. He was scheduled to start Game 3 on Thursday against the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series, but that game turned out not to be necessary. The 36-year-old last pitched more than a week ago, giving up two runs in 5 2/3 innings against these same Rays on Sept. 23.
Carlos Rodon also has plenty of rest, however, and even ace Cam Schlittler should be relatively fresh, having not pitched since Game 1 against the Red Sox on Tuesday. Rodon, Schlittler and Max Fried all have better numbers this season than Cole, who missed all of last season after undergoing Tommy John surgery. But Cole has the name and the track record.
Cole has started 12 playoff games in his Yankees career, with a 2.93 ERA. He's started 22 playoff games in total with a 2.77 ERA and 1.020 WHIP that reveal how misleading his 7-8 career postseason record is.
Going solely by this season, the Yankees might have better options. But Cole has the longest resume of success, and on Saturday, he'll have the ball.
More MLB: Knicks Star Makes Crazy Comment Involving God, Cam Schlittler

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] An open letter to Yankees fans who wanted Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone gone | Klapisch
item.dc:creator: Bob Klapisch
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — This is an open letter to anyone who's railed against Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone over the years. That's a huge swath of Yankees fans – maybe all of them. So let's call this a mass mailing. The Yankees are a step closer to the World Series for two reasons. The first was the Red Sox's glaring deficits. Scoring just two runs in 18 innings, they just weren't good enough to hang with the Yankees. If the Wild Card Series were replayed 10 times, the Yankees would likely win ni
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — This is an open letter to anyone who's railed against Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone over the years. That's a huge swath of Yankees fans – maybe all of them. So let's call this a mass mailing.
The Yankees are a step closer to the World Series for two reasons. The first was the Red Sox's glaring deficits. Scoring just two runs in 18 innings, they just weren't good enough to hang with the Yankees. If the Wild Card Series were replayed 10 times, the Yankees would likely win nine.
The second reason is why we're here today. Although this isn't the greatest Yankees roster of the last 20 years, it is remarkably well-constructed and well-managed. That's another way of saying Cashman and Boone have done their jobs well. They deserve credit for that.
The question is whether the critics will ever reconsider. I have my doubts. The folks who've been demanding Cashman's and Boone's firing for almost a decade aren't exactly open to reasonable dialogue. They're dug in so deep that one of them, who just happens to be an old college buddy, insisted, "Anyone could've beaten the Red Sox. That's how much they sucked."
My friend isn't entirely wrong — at least about Boston's non-existent offense. It's hard to believe this was the same team that went on a 14-game winning streak this summer.
But to suggest that any manager with Cam Schlittler as their ace and Ben Rice hitting lasers could've taken down the Sox is flat-out wrong. That's like saying all managers are the same. Their only job is to fill out the lineup card and talk to the TV cameras after the game.
Not quite.
Managers have personality traits that can enhance the roster's potential. Joe Torre, laid-back in a streetwise sort of way, was the perfect candidate to replace the hyper-involved Buck Showalter. Torre was never loud, but still tough enough to absorb late owner George Steinbrenner's manic behavior.
When Torre's enthusiasm for managing waned by 2006, Joe Girardi — ultra-prepared, obsessed with process — represented the pendulum swinging in the other direction. And when the next generation of Yankees decided Girardi was just too uptight and disconnected from the clubhouse, Boone won over Cashman because he was smart, calm and relatable.
I realize fans no longer care about Boone's personality. Not even his .582 winning percentage — second only to the Dodgers' Dave Roberts among active managers — gets the credit it deserves. What matters are championships. Boone has none since he replaced Girardi in 2018. In the Bronx, that's 0-for-forever.
That doesn't mean Boone is a bad manager. He checks so many other boxes that have kept the Yankees competitive. The players like Boone, but more importantly, they trust his instincts. In fact, Boone had a terrific series against Boston, embarrassing Chad Tracy, his counterpart in the other dugout.
Boone didn't make any significant mistakes against the Sox. His most important decision of the series came in Game 1.
After allowing Schlittler to throw 117 pitches, Boone summoned Paul Blackburn in the seventh inning to protect a 2-0 lead. Facing Ceddanne Rafaela with the tying run at the plate, Blackburn induced an inning-ending double play. The Yankees went on to score seven runs in the next two innings.
Tracy, on the other hand, made two decisions that doomed Boston. In both games, he pulled his starter in the fifth inning with two outs and the Sox trailing 1-0 — first Payton Tolle, then Sonny Gray. The Yankees promptly destroyed reliever Erik Miller on both occasions.
Several Sox players, including Gray and Willson Contreras, have since second-guessed Tracy's strategy and the team's overall direction.
You don't hear that kind of anti-Boone sniping in the Yankees' clubhouse. Even Boone's handling of Aaron Judge's irritation at being left off the Wild Card roster showed finesse. Boone demonstrated he was in control without making a show of pulling rank.
One former Yankee texted me the other day about the back-and-forth between Boone and Judge. He believes the episode showed how much Boone has grown on the job.
"All (Boone) said was, 'We don't expect Judge to be back,'" the former Yankee said. "That's Boone's way of telling the rest of the players, 'It's time for you to step up. Don't sit here waiting for Judge to rescue you.' It was a positive message."
Of course, it takes the right kind of players to understand that. The Yankees are a stable group. Even Jose Caballero, who came to the Yankees with the reputation of being a rogue element, has fallen into line.
That's where Cashman comes in. He made one right call after another in assembling this 93-win roster. The bullpen is airtight; the gamble on trading for closer David Bednar has worked to perfection. The GM made the smart move by promoting George Lombard Jr. this summer instead of waiting until September or 2027. And the rotation, finally healthy, is the Yankees' best since 2009.
MORE BY BOB KLAPISCH
All it took was one more piece — Max Fried. His signing in free agency in 2025 had Cashman's fingerprints all over it.
Beat the Rays, and the Yankees are back in the AL Championship Series. Win there, and they're back in the World Series for the second time in three years. At that point, those haters just might admit Cashman and Boone had something to do with it.
I'm such a nice guy that I'll give my friend a chance to admit he was wrong all along.

item.title: [whec.com] Having bashed Boston without Judge, Yankees turn attention to AL Division Series vs. pesky Rays
item.dc:creator: Kiley Wren
item.description: Having bashed Boston without Judge, Yankees turn attention to AL Division Series vs. pesky Rays NEW YORK (AP) — Having bashed Boston without Aaron Judge, the New York Yankees face a far different task when they face the pesky Tampa Bay Rays in an AL Division Series starting Saturday, Riding powerful pitching led by Cam Schlitter and Max Fried, Yankees batters broke though just enough against Red Sox starters and beat up Boston’s bullpen in sweeping their rival in the Wild Card Series. “We’re goi
item.content:encoded:
Having bashed Boston without Judge, Yankees turn attention to AL Division Series vs. pesky Rays
NEW YORK (AP) — Having bashed Boston without Aaron Judge, the New York Yankees face a far different task when they face the pesky Tampa Bay Rays in an AL Division Series starting Saturday,
Riding powerful pitching led by Cam Schlitter and Max Fried, Yankees batters broke though just enough against Red Sox starters and beat up Boston’s bullpen in sweeping their rival in the Wild Card Series.
“We’re going to continue to rely on amazing starting pitching like we have all year,” Ben Rice said after Wednesday night’s 9-2 win. ”Especially in the postseason, that’s what you need.”
Schlittler and Fried combined to go 2-0 with a 0.73 ERA against the Red Sox with 16 strikeouts and two walks in 12 1/3 innings.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone must decide whether to open against the Rays with Gerrit Cole, who was set to start a Game 3 against Boston, or Carlos Rodón.
“Obviously, Gerrit’s lined up for that. Carlos is very much in play for that,” Boone said. “We have a ton of confidence in both guys. I think they’re both throwing the ball really well.”
Boone said it was possible Schlittler, Fried, Cole and Rodón all will start against the Rays. New York’s starters led the major leagues with a 3.30 ERA.
“That’s been the biggest strength for us throughout the year,” Boone said. “It sustained us. It got us through some difficult times. And I feel like they’re all in a good place right now.”
New York’s best-of-five series against the Rays has an extra off day between Games 1 and 2, allowing Schlittler to start the second game and come back on normal rest for a Game 5.
Whether Judge will return to the lineup remains unclear.
Sidelined since Sept. 16 by a strained right calf, Judge has resumed hitting.
“Saturday’s a long ways away, but I’m doing everything I can, all morning, night, during the game, everything to prepare myself to be ready to go,” Judge said. “So I want to be in there. So we’ll see what happens.”
Tampa Bay won the season series 7-6 en route to an AL-best 98-64 record, their runners often spinning around the bases like a roulette ball going around the wheel. The Rays were sixth in the major leagues with a .326 on-base percentage and tied for second with 164 stolen bases.
Rays batters struck out the fewest times in the major leagues at 1,145, an average of about two per game fewer than the Yankees.
Because they won the AL East and had a bye, the Rays will enter the series with five days’ rest — which some in baseball is convinced causes rust.
“The alternative is playing three must-win games or two out of three. I’ll take where we’re at,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said.
Rays left-handed pitchers held lefty batters to a .205 average during the regular season. Yankees lefty batters hit .500 (11 for 22) against Boston southpaws.
“They faced so many guys for months there where we were very left-handed, where in the fifth inning every day it was one lefty and then another one because that’s how they attack us,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “So I’d like to think some of that familiarity and reps and all that prepared us well.”
New York was second in the majors with 223 home runs, three behind Houston. What was often a home-run-or-bust batting order diversified in the Wild Card Series.
Homegrown players — Rice, Spencer Jones, George Lombard Jr., Anthony Volpe and Austin Wells — combined for 11 RBIs.
“The young guys have done a tremendous job,” outfielder Cody Bellinger said. “It’s been fun to watch. It’s fun to watch them grow and they’ve been a huge part of our success.”

Tonight, Max Fried will become the sixth pitcher in MLB history to make at least one postseason start in seven consecutive years (2020-2026), joining Greg Maddux (nine), Andy Pettitte (nine), Tom Glavine (eig
item.content:encoded:
Max Fried added his name to an exclusive list of MLB postseason legends Wednesday night. The Yankees left-hander became the seventh pitcher in MLB history to make at least one postseason start in seven consecutive years, joining some of the greatest playoff pitchers the sport has ever seen.
Tonight, Max Fried will become the sixth pitcher in MLB history to make at least one postseason start in seven consecutive years (2020-2026), joining Greg Maddux (nine), Andy Pettitte (nine), Tom Glavine (eight), Clayton Kershaw (eight) and Roger Clemens (seven). pic.twitter.com/ZDBRWyYOoN
— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) September 30, 2026
Fried joins an incredible list of postseason legends
Fried’s streak began in 2020 and continued through Wednesday night’s Game 2 start against the Boston Red Sox. That gives him seven consecutive seasons with at least one postseason start, putting him alongside an impressive group of pitchers.
The list includes Tom Glavine, Greg Maddux, Andy Pettitte, Clayton Kershaw, John Smoltz and Roger Clemens.
Fried’s achievement is particularly notable because he has now established himself as a consistent postseason starter across multiple organizations and stages of his career.
Fried delivered when the Yankees needed him
Fried didn’t simply make history by taking the mound. He delivered one of his best postseason performances in a Yankees uniform.
The left-hander allowed just three hits and one earned run over six innings against Boston, walking one and striking out six on 98 pitches. The Yankees went on to win 9-2 and complete a two-game sweep of the Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series.
After the Yankees selected Cam Schlittler to start Game 1, Fried followed him in Game 2 and helped send New York into the AL Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays.
For Fried, Wednesday night was another chapter in an already impressive postseason résumé — and another reminder that his October experience now puts him in the company of some legendary MLB playoff pitchers.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have gotten off to an incredibly fast start to the 2026 MLB postseason. They made quick work of their arch rival Boston Red Sox in the best-of-three Wild Card series, outscoring them 18-2 in a 2-0 series win.
New York will next meet their division winner Tampa Bay Rays in the best-of-five ALDS. That series begins Saturday in Tampa Bay and continues there on Monday before coming back to the Bronx next Wednesday.
Once again, the Yankees will head into the division series on the heels of a lights-out performance from their ace right-hander Cam Schlittler. In Game 1 against Boston, he hurled 6 ⅓ scoreless innings while racking up 10 strikeouts.
Potential reinforcements
Following Wednesday’s series conclusion in Game 2, Schlittler spoke on currently injured outfielder Aaron Judge. Per Greg Joyce of the New York Post, the ace said that he believes Judge is the best player in baseball and that the club will only get stronger upon his return.
The 34-year-old appeared in just 66 games this season, missing a huge chunk of time through the summer before briefly returning in September. He unfortunately suffered a moderate calf strain Sept. 16 and has been on the injured list since.
When he was on the field, Judge admittedly was not quite playing like himself. Across 285 plate appearances, he slashed .241/.360/.511 (.871 OPS) with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs.
With the ALDS versus the Rays beginning Saturday, that will mark 17 days since Judge suffered the calf strain. Only time will tell whether he will be healthy enough to play, though there is some serious doubt on that.
Series outlook
For the Yankees side of things, it will be either righty Gerrit Cole or lefty Carlos Rodón on the mound for Game 1 of the ALDS. That choice from the club will come out in the next couple of days.
Schlittler will be on five days’ rest to pitch Game 2 on Monday, before lefty Max Fried gets the ball in Game 3 back in the Bronx. Beyond that, a prospective Games 4 and 5 do not have pitching probables.
Surprisingly enough, despite the two teams’ competitiveness over the last several years, they have yet to meet in the postseason following a normal 162-game season. It will be the first time each club has headed to the other’s venue for playoff baseball in their histories.

item.content:encoded:
There obviously are plenty of Yankees fans who aren’t enamored with Aaron Boone’s managerial body of work, but let’s give the man some flowers here for his and his team’s performance in their wild-card series blowout of the Red Sox.
Boone, still looking for his first World Series title in nine seasons on the job, managed circles around Boston’s Chad Tracy in the two-game sweep in The Bronx. That is indisputable.
Tracy’s hiring after Alex Cora was canned in April following a 10-17 start was largely credited with the Red Sox’s 32-5 run that vaulted them back into playoff position this summer. But he looked like a panicked manager in quick-hooking starters Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray with matching 1-0 deficits in the fifth inning of each game — only to watch the Yankees hammer his bullpen for an 18-2 aggregate drubbing in their two wins.
Boone certainly benefitted from starters Cam Schlittler and Max Fried pitching to a 0.73 ERA with one run allowed over a combined 12 ⅓ innings.

item.title: [wral.com] Fried, Bellinger and García lead Yankees over Red Sox 9-2 for 2-game Wild Card Series sweep
item.dc:creator: RONALD BLUM
item.description: NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston. Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep. Other WRAL Top Stories “We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said. New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series start
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston.
Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep.
Other WRAL Top Stories
“We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
“The fans were electric from the first pitch and the boys were hungry. We got a young, hungry team here," Yankees captain Aaron Judge said as teammates sprayed him with bubbly during the clubhouse celebration. “This makes me feel young every single time.”
Judge missed this series because of a calf injury and isn't sure whether he will play against the Rays, who beat New York 7-6 in the season series.
“Saturday’s a long ways away," he said.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston's 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke open the game with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out leading off — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBIs that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst that put New York ahead 8-1.
“Step one,” said Bellinger, who caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay, a 2000 Yankees World Series champion. “Now we got to go into Tampa and play against a tough team."
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, lost last year's wild-card matchup after defeating the Yankees in the opener.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there was quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series and that ended for us tonight, so it’s frustrating,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “There’s a lot of things you can say, but in the moment right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it’s going to take some time to get over that.”
Boston, which also got a seventh-inning homer from Nick Sogard off Will Warren, was missing leadoff hitter Roman Anthony because of a hand injury. The Red Sox were held to a .117 average in the series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and outscored 18-2.
New York hit .382 in the series. Boston's bullpen had a 20.25 ERA.
“We played great baseball in a lot of ways here, obviously anchored by our two great starters," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Yankees batters hit .450 (9 for 20) with runners in scoring position after finishing 19th among the 30 teams with a .246 RISP during the regular season.
“I feel like it’s a whole new level from regular season to these last two days,” Austin Wells said.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García's fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just relieved.
Gray was disappointed he wasn't allowed to face Bellinger.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. "I would’ve liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. And, yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. So I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted.”
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger's homer.
"I can’t believe they were willing to face a guy like Belli with men on base there," Rice said.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year's Wild Card Series opener, hadn't pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation when he bounced a sweeper off Adley Rutschman's chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled that Jones was out. The Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner's office.
“I couldn’t believe he was there,” Boone said. "I saw the ball squirt away a little bit. I didn’t think that much of it, and looked up and I was, like, 'Oh, he’s safe.'''
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Wells' sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout and Rice, who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“Definitely wasn’t sharp from the get-go but just wanted to challenge them, not try to give any free passes, especially in the first inning," Fried said.
After a night of celebration and a day off, the Yankees will head to Florida on Friday.
“There’s just so much more to do,” Bellinger said after the big night with his father on hand. “So obviously enjoy the moment, understand how cool it is, but keep on going.”
Up Next
New York RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.
___

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — For about 10 minutes, there was a ballgame.
The window opened around 9:56 p.m. ET on Wednesday. Boston first baseman Willson Contreras sliced a Max Fried fastball through the crisp Bronx air into the first row in right for a solo home run. That cut New York's lead in half. For the first time in this best-of-three wild-card series between longtime rivals, a Red Sox hitter touched home plate. And so, a glimmer of hope flickered in the visiting dugout as Game 2 flipped to the bottom of the sixth.
By 10:06 p.m., when rookie George Lombard Jr. laced an RBI single over the second baseman's head, that flame had already begun to falter. By the end of the inning, it was thoroughly extinguished.
Ten Yankees hitters came to the plate in the bottom of the sixth; six scored. Last year's AL Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, injured for nearly the entire regular season, entered as a reliever and did not record an out (though he did strike out a batter). Boston's most trusted setup man, Garrett Whitlock, then entered the ballgame to serve up the final blow: a moon-scraping, three-run homer via Cody Bellinger that pushed New York's lead to seven.
Yankee Stadium rumbled as Bellinger's ball returned to Earth. Libations sprung into the sky like a Bellagio fountain of booze. Popcorn rained from the heavens. Bellinger rounded the sacks and entered the dugout to a tunnel of high-fives and atta-boys. The rest of this lopsided laugher was merely epilogue. By the ninth inning, Yankee fans were serenading the defeated Sox with "na, na, na, na, hey, hey, hey, goodbye." A few minutes later, they were hollering Sinatra's "New York, New York" as the Yankees strolled onto the diamond in a casual celebration.
No doubt — not a crumb — was left as to which is the better team.
"Total domination," a Yankees employee could be heard saying to a colleague in the champagne-soaked afterparty.
Predictably, New York skipper Aaron Boone offered Boston its flowers, but it was incredibly telling that the first question asked to him at his postgame media conference was: "Were you surprised by the margins of victory?"
"Yes," Boone, ever the politician, replied. "As I said, kind of all year, but even going into this series, that was a scary team to us, especially as well as they pitch. So for us to have the offensive outbreaks that we had here these last two nights and late, credit to those guys."
No more than 30 minutes later, Boone could be seen stampeding past the Yankees' clubhouse with neither a shirt nor a worry in the world. Nothing about this wild-card matchup provided any reason for him or any other Yankees employee to view the Red Sox as a scary team. No, this was a drubbing.
The Yankees outscored the Red Sox 18-2 across the two games. Boston mustered seven total hits, the fewest ever in a wild-card series (this format was implemented in 2022). It was a damning, telling offensive performance by a lineup that lacked both the impact and the depth of a legitimate championship contender. And while the Sox certainly felt the absence of Roman Anthony — the young slugger was scratched from the roster after suffering a wrist injury in Game 1 — not even a resuscitated, cryogenically unfrozen Ted Williams could've helped this Boston ballclub.
"You're thinking we're going to play closer games," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy admitted postgame. "They swung the bats extremely well. You've got to give them credit. It was frustrating."
Also frustrating, for Tracy, must have been the noticeable chasm in talent between the two clubs. The Red Sox drew deserved plaudits ahead of the series for their run-prevention prowess. And yet, on paper, the Yankees' rotation looked far more dangerous. And that's how it played out, with soon-to-be Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler dicing in Game 1 and Fried cruising in Game 2.
New York's decision to roster just 10 pitchers for this series was also an indication of the organization's immense level of confidence in its staff, particularly its starters. Why enter the battle with an army when a small special-ops unit can do the job?
"That's been the biggest strength for us throughout the year," Boone said of his team's rotation. "It sustained us. It got us through some difficult times. And I feel like they're all in a good place right now."
The Yankees' lineup is also clearly in a very good place. With captain Aaron Judge off the roster and watching from the dugout in a hoodie, New York's offense impressed. In both games, the Bombers needed a few innings to get revved up but eventually bludgeoned Boston's bullpen into submission. They tallied 26 total hits, the most by the Yanks in a two-game playoff span since 2004.
Judge's status for the ALDS against Tampa Bay remains a mystery. Fellow injured large man Giancarlo Stanton was on the roster for the wild-card round but wasn't called upon for a plate appearance. The Rays will likely present a stiffer challenge than whatever this was, but New York's lineup is humming at the perfect time.
Boston, meanwhile, didn't even get to play October baseball. When closer David Bednar punched out Caleb Durbin to conclude the proceedings, the clock read 11:14 p.m. ET.
September lived on. The Red Sox did not.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Yankees set sights on tougher Rays team after embarrassing Red Sox with Wild Card sweep

item.content:encoded:
Ever since the Yankees acquired Luis García Jr. on Aug. 3, the former National pictured what postseason baseball would look and feel like. He talked about it with his new teammates, many of whom spoke from experience that he did not have.
The New York native got his first taste on Tuesday, going 0-for-1 off the bench in the Yankees’ easy 9-0 win over the Red Sox in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series. But on Wednesday, he made his mark in his first postseason start, hammering a Sonny Gray sweeper in the fourth inning of Game 2.
The solo shot jumpstarted an offense that ensured there would not be a Game 3, as the Yankees cruised to a 9-2 victory after García got them on the board. Complete with an animated bat flip, he sparked the dugout’s first celebration of the night.
“It’s unforgettable to be in the middle of all that,” said García, draped in a towel. “I’m sure it’s something I’m not gonna forget.”
With Cody Bellinger adding a three-run homer in the sixth and Max Fried holding Boston to one earned run over six innings, the party eventually moved to the mound and then the home clubhouse at Yankee Stadium. There, the boozy Bombers celebrated a rather smooth sweep of their embarrassed archrivals with bubbly and beers.
“That was a scary team to us, especially as well as they pitch. So for us to have the offensive outbreaks that we had here these last two nights and late, credit to those guys,” Aaron Boone said. “That was very satisfying to play that well in these two games.”
Now another division foe awaits in the ALDS, and a tougher one at that.
The Yankees already know how formidable the Rays, their next playoff opponent, are, as the pinstripers failed to win the American League East for the second straight season because of Tampa Bay. Despite a luxury tax payroll that fell $228.9 million short of the Yankees’, the Rays finished the season with the AL’s best record at 98-64 and earned a first-round bye in the postseason.
The Yankees’ meanwhile, ended up 93-68, settling for the top Wild Card spot and a rematch with the overmatched Red Sox.
Cam Schlittler, who shoved in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, said it was “frustrating” to lose the AL East to the Rays, but he tipped his hat to them, too.
“They’ve been great all year,” said Schlittler, who is expected to start Game 2 of the ALDS. “We had opportunities to take the [division] lead, and we couldn’t get that done.”
But, he said, “We’re on a roll at the right time.”
While the Yankees are hot after beating up on Boston, the rested Rays, who celebrated their division crown in the Bronx on Sept. 22, have home field advantage in the best-of-five ALDS. Carried by its quickness, pitching staff and Junior Caminero’s rising star, Tampa also has the comfort of knowing that it won the season series against the Yankees, 7-6.
“They bring speed to the game,” said Carlos Rodón, a candidate to start Game 1 of the ALDS alongside Gerrit Cole. “They have some good pitching. They play good defense. They’ll take the extra bag. They’re gonna be running. They’re gonna be bunting. You don’t see that in the game much anymore, but it’s worked for them. They’re a solid club. They play well, so it should be a good series.”
“It’s going to be a tough series,” Bellinger added.
If the Yankees are lucky, a reinforcement or two will join them in Florida for the showdown. Ryan Weathers, working his way back from a flexor strain as a reliever, could be one of them.
Getting Aaron Judge back would be a much bigger deal, however, after the back-to-back MVP watched the Wild Card Series from the bench in a jacket and a hoodie.
The Yankees managed to take Boston down without the captain after a right calf strain kept Judge off their Wild Card roster. On Wednesday, Boone said it’s “too early to tell” if Judge will be available for Game 1 of the ALDS, which begins on Saturday.
The manager added that Tampa Bay’s turfed Tropicana Field “could” factor into the Yankees’ decision with Judge having yet to run the bases. That call, however, is still a few days away from being made after the Yankees bought themselves some time with a quick Wild Card Series.
Judge, who lobbied to be on the Wild Card roster, declined to talk about his potential availability for the ALDS. But the slugger, who also missed 99 days with a fractured rib this season, did take a moment to praise what his peers have accomplished thus far.
“I’ve been so proud of these guys,” Judge said as he dodged champagne spritzes. “I’ve been out for quite a long time this season, and they never wavered. They never took a step back. They just kept going forward.”
“When the Yankees win, we all win. So it doesn’t matter if you played, didn’t play, hit the game-winning hit, pitched a shutout. We’re all wearing ‘NY’ in this room. That’s why we’re all celebrating together.”

Fried earned the win in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series against the Red Sox on Wednesday. He struck out six and allowed one run on three hits and one walk over six innings.
The veteran left-hander was working on a shutout until Willson Contreras launched a two-out, solo homer during the top of the sixth inning, which spelled an end to his day after the Yankees erupted for six runs in the bottom of the frame. It's the second straight season Fried shut down Boston in the wild-card round, as he fired 6.1 scoreless frames in Game 1 of that series last year. He missed time in 2026 due to elbow issues but still made 20 regular-season starts and had a 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 104:33 K:BB across 112.2 innings.

item.title: [bostonherald.com] Yankees humiliate, eliminate Red Sox in Wild Card for second straight year
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: NEW YORK – As the Red Sox were outscored 18-2 and eliminated in a two-game Wild Card sweep by the Yankees on Tuesday (9-0) and Wednesday night (9-2) at Yankee Stadium, the aura of ‘Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me’ was brutal and undeniable. A week after the 2025 Red Sox fell to their eternal rivals in the Wild Card round in the Bronx, including a shutout in the deciding Game 3, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow sat in the Fenway Park interview room, flanked by manager A
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – As the Red Sox were outscored 18-2 and eliminated in a two-game Wild Card sweep by the Yankees on Tuesday (9-0) and Wednesday night (9-2) at Yankee Stadium, the aura of ‘Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me’ was brutal and undeniable.
A week after the 2025 Red Sox fell to their eternal rivals in the Wild Card round in the Bronx, including a shutout in the deciding Game 3, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow sat in the Fenway Park interview room, flanked by manager Alex Cora and team president Sam Kennedy, and declared that adding home-run power to the lineup would be a top priority for 2025-26 offseason.
Breslow reiterated as much throughout the ensuing months, while the front office failed to sign any of the top free-agent hitters, including Alex Bregman, who opted out of his Red Sox contract and went to the Chicago Cubs after the former refused to give him a no-trade clause.
The week after Bregman signed his five-year deal with the Cubs in mid-January, Breslow inked left-hander Ranger Suarez to a five-year contract. Breslow then proclaimed at Suarez’s introductory presser, “I don’t think there’s a question anymore that the identity of our team, the strength of our team, is going to be our pitching.”
And it was. So much so that when the Red Sox and Yankees met in the Wild Card round again this week, the Boston bats were silent as the grave.
“Uncompetitive. We got boat-raced,” veteran infielder Isiah Kiner-Falefa told reporters postgame. “To lose in the Wild Card is unacceptable.”
Hitting, or lack thereof, was far from the only problem. Chad Tracy’s inexperience was on display, particularly where pitching decisions were concerned. The new Red Sox skipper managed both contests, not like the must-win games they were, but like a Triple-A game, where there is endless runway because the priority is player development and any victories are simply a nice bonus.
Yankees batters did plenty of damage, and the Red Sox played non-urgent defense at times. But offense remained Boston’s most glaring issue, because it was the key offseason need left unmet.
Yankees southpaw Max Fried allowed one earned run on three hits, walked one and struck out six over six innings (98 pitches, 62 strikes).
Red Sox starter Sonny Gray was largely dominant in 4 2/3 innings. He allowed two earned runs on six hits, issued zero walks and struck out five.
But for the second straight game, Tracy pulled his starter with two outs in the fifth in favor of left-hander Erik Miller, who had allowed earned runs in four of his last five regular-season appearances, and immediately given up a home run to Ben Rice in Game 1.
Rice scored on Miller again in Game 2, in the form of a start-ending single off Gray and Cody Bellinger’s RBI single off the Sox southpaw.
But the true implosion came when Garrett Crochet took the mound in the bottom of the sixth, his first game at any level since April 25. All four Yankees batters reached before Tracy called upon righty Garrett Whitlock. An Austin Wells RBI sacrifice fly and Ryan McMahon RBI groundout increased the lead to 5-1. After an intentional walk to Rice, Bellinger took Whitlock deep to put a long-over game firmly in the ground.
New York out-hit Boston 14-4 on Wednesday night. The losing team managed two walks, struck out eight times, were 0 for 2 with runners in scoring position, and left four men on base.
The 2026 Red Sox took steps forward. Pitching was largely better, the postseason notwithstanding. Defense was markedly better, an irony that cannot be lost on Cora, who spent years lamenting his team’s poor defense, only to see them improve right before and after his late-April firing.
But the Red Sox also took steps backward this year; some baffling, some beyond their control, others by their own design.
They finished this regular season 87-75, two losses worse than last year.
The offense was markedly worse. The 2025 Red Sox collectively slashed .254/.324/.421 with 324 doubles, and 186 home runs in the regular season. They finished this regular season with a .245/.319/.397 line, 285 doubles, and 163 home runs. (Bregman finished the regular season with 28 home runs, more than any player on the Red Sox roster; he drove the point home, literally, by hitting the last two off Boston pitchers in Game 162 on Sunday.)
True, the Red Sox struck out significantly less this year – 1,326 down from 1,419 – but they also finished one walk shy of last year’s total (518).
Above all, they scored 689 runs this year, a whopping 97 fewer than last year.
The two things the 2025 Red Sox needed most in October, runs and homer power, were in even shorter supply on Wednesday night. As a result, their “October run” came to an end before the month even began.
The 2026 Red Sox were a horror show at both start and finish.
But in the immortal words of the movie “Grease,” “Oh! Those summer nights.”

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Cody Bellinger hit a three-run homer during a six-run sixth inning and finished with four RBIs as the New York Yankees pulled away for a 9-2 rout of the Boston Red Sox on Wednesday and a two-game sweep of an American League wild-card series.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox in the wild-card round for the second straight year and were significantly more prolific at the plate than last year, when they needed three games to advance.
Despite the absence of Aaron Judge, who has a strained right calf, New York scored 18 runs and totaled 26 hits in the series to advance to the AL Division Series against the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays. The best-of-five ALDS begins Saturday in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Bellinger capped New York’s big inning by hitting a 1-0 changeup from Garrett Whitlock into the right-center-field seats after the Red Sox opted to intentionally walk Ben Rice. The blast pushed New York’s lead to 8-1.
In the fifth, Bellinger chopped an RBI single against left-hander Erik Miller over second baseman Nick Sogard’s head to give the Yankees a 2-0 lead.
New York’s Max Fried (1-0) followed Cam Schlittler’s dominance in the series opener by allowing one run on three hits in six innings on Wednesday. Fried struck out six and walked one.
Luis Garcia Jr. also homered for the Yankees, connecting against Sonny Gray’s 1-2 sweeper while leading off the fourth to open the scoring.
The Yankees sent 10 to the plate against Garrett Crochet and Whitlock in their big inning, getting things started with rookie Spencer Jones hustling around the bases.
Jones started things by reaching on a wild-pitch strikeout when he beat catcher Adley Rutschman’s throw by a step on a call that was overturned on replay after the Yankees challenged. Jones then stole second, advanced to third on Rutschman’s throwing error and scored on George Lombard Jr.’s single.
After singles by Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham loaded the bases, Whitlock replaced Crochet. Austin Wells lifted a sacrifice fly, and Ryan McMahon followed with a soft RBI groundout for a 5-1 lead.
Willson Contreras homered off Fried in the sixth, and Nick Sogard homered off Will Warren in the seventh.
Wells added an RBI single in the bottom of the seventh.
Gray (0-1) allowed two runs on six hits in 4 2/3 innings, with five strikeouts and no walks. Crochet made his first appearance since April 25, having recovered from a shoulder ailment, and was charged with four runs without recording an out.
The Red Sox finished with seven hits in the series and experienced a disappointing end to a season where they overcame firing their manager in April and having a 32-46 record in late June. Boston vaulted into playoff contention with a 32-5 surge that included a 15-game winning streak but struggled at the plate in the final month.
