item.content:encoded:
Fried, Yankees sweep Red Sox in AL wild card series with 9-2 win
Max Fried shut down the Boston Red Sox again in October, and the New York Yankees backed him with a sixth-inning offensive eruption to complete a two-game AL Wild Card Series sweep with a 9-2 win Wednesday night.
Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered as the Yankees pulled away after Boston briefly cut into the lead on Willson Contreras’ homer, which ended the Red Sox’s 26-inning postseason scoreless streak. New York was clinging to a 2-1 advantage before breaking the game open with six runs in the sixth inning.
The inning began in unusual fashion when Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out leading off, a play that stood after a video review. Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth in a half-inning that also included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and an intentional walk to Ben Rice before Bellinger’s three-run homer capped the outburst and made it 8-1.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start. His fourth-inning homer put New York ahead. Bellinger, who had four RBIs, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-hander Erik Miller just after Miller entered in relief. Bellinger also caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who won a World Series with New York in 2000.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series opener, had not pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation. In the sixth, he bounced a sweeper off Contreras’ chest. Contreras picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled out, but the Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner’s office.
After the reversal, Jones stole second and went to third when Contreras’ throw skipped into center field. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single. Austin Wells’ sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock made it 4-1, Ryan McMahon added an RBI groundout, and Rice — who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener — was intentionally walked before Bellinger “reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.”
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried allowed three hits over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta. He struck out six and walked one, and has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in two Wild Card Series against Boston.
Nick Sogard hit a solo homer off Will Warren in the seventh for Boston.
The Red Sox, who reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, were eliminated by the Yankees in the first round for the second straight year. Boston hit .117 in the two-game series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and was outscored 18-2.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday. Right-hander Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Yankees complete sweep of Red Sox, advance to ALDS
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.description: By RONALD BLUM AP Baseball Writer NEW YORK — Max Fried dominated Boston in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the New York Yankees romped over the Red Sox, 9-2, on Wednesday night for a two-game sweep of their American League Wild Card Series. Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston’s 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke the game open with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild
item.content:encoded:
By RONALD BLUM AP Baseball Writer
NEW YORK — Max Fried dominated Boston in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the New York Yankees romped over the Red Sox, 9-2, on Wednesday night for a two-game sweep of their American League Wild Card Series.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston’s 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke the game open with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out leading off – with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBIs that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst that put New York ahead 8-1.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in a best-of-five AL Division Series starting Saturday in Florida.
“Step one,” Bellinger said. “Now we got to go into Tampa and play against a tough team.”
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, was eliminated by the Yankees in the first round for the second straight year.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there was quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series and that ended for us tonight, so it’s frustrating,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “There’s a lot of things you can say, but in the moment right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it’s going to take some time to get over that.”
Boston was held to a .117 batting average in the series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and was outscored 18-2.
“That was very satisfying to play that well in these two games,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “They played great and beat a really good team that deserves a lot of credit for, was down and out in the middle of the season and fought their way back to being a no-doubt into the playoffs by the end.”
A day after Cam Schlittler pitched New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with the Atlanta Braves.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García’s fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just relieved. Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay Bellinger, who won a World Series with New York in 2000.
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger’s homer.
“Baseball can be a wacky sport,” Bellinger said.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series opener, hadn’t pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation when he bounced a sweeper off catcher Adley Rutschman’s chest. Rutschman picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled that Jones was out. The Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner’s office.
“I couldn’t believe he was there,” Boone said. “I saw the ball squirt away a little bit. I didn’t think that much of it, and looked up and I was, like, ‘Oh, he’s safe.’”
Jones, who debuted in May, scored three runs in the series to tie fellow rookie George Lombard Jr. and Rice for the team lead.
“It’s a great thing to be able to get on the bases I guess anyway possible,” Jones said. “I was always told if you run hard, good things are going to happen and that turned out to be the case.”
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Lombard singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Austin Wells’ sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout and Rice, who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.
Fried, a former Harvard-Westlake star, struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12⅓ innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“Definitely wasn’t sharp from the get-go but just wanted to challenge them, not try to give any free passes, especially in the first inning,” Fried said.
Nick Sogard hit a solo homer off Will Warren in the seventh.
UP NEXT
New York right-hander Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Cam Schlittler fanned 10 in 6 1/3 dominant innings while Ben Rice homered twice and drove in six runs as the New York Yankees pulled away for a 9-0 rout of the Boston Red Sox in Game 1 of an American League wild-card series on Tuesday night.
The Yankees can close out the best-of-three series on Wednesday when Max Fried pitches. Sonny Gray will try to extend Boston’s season to Game 3 on Thursday.
Nearly a year after fanning 12 and allowing five hits in eight scoreless innings in Game 3 of last year’s wild-card series, Schlittler (1-0) was equally as sharp in his third career postseason start to help the Yankees get the upper hand.
Schlittler allowed just three baserunners, two singles and a walk. His 117 pitches were not only a career high but the most by a Yankee in a postseason game since CC Sabathia threw a 121-pitch complete game in Game 5 of the 2012 AL Division Series against the Baltimore Orioles.
Schlittler threw 77 pitches for strikes while going up against the team he grew up rooting for in Walpole, Mass.
A native of Cohasset, Mass., Rice hit a solo homer for a 2-0 lead in the fifth off left-handed reliever Erik Miller and added an RBI single in the seventh. He capped a five-run eighth by launching a grand slam off Brayan Bello over the right-center-field fence.
Rice went 4-for-5 and had New York’s first four-hit postseason game since Gleyber Torres accomplished the feat in Game 1 of the 2020 wild-card series at Cleveland.
Catcher Austin Wells helped Schlittler by winning an ABS challenge on Wilyer Abreu for a called third strike to end the first inning and hit an RBI single with two on in the second against Boston starter Payton Tolle.
Rookie George Lombard Jr. had three hits and two runs.
Tolle allowed one run on five hits in 4 2/3 innings. The left-hander struck out four, walked one and threw 58 of 83 pitches for strikes.
Paul Blackburn (1 2/3 innings) and John Schreiber (one inning) finished the Yankees’ three-hitter.

We’ve already got goosebumps.
For the seventh time in MLB history, the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox are meeting in the playoffs.
This time around, the Bronx Bombers and BoSox will go toe-to-toe in the Wild Card round in a best-of-three series that determines who gets to take on the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
The trio of games will all take place at the Bronx’s Yankee Stadium. They’re slated go down:
Game 1
Tuesday, Sept. 29
8 p.m.

Game 2

Game 3

If you’d like to be there, the lowest price we could find on tickets for any one games was $129 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $131 and $135 including fees for the other two contests.
Over the course of the regular season, New York and Boston met 13 times; the Yankees took seven of those showdowns. In their final battle, the Yankees walloped the Sox 16-1 on Aug. 30. Heliot Ramos, Paul Goldschmidt, José Caballero and Austin Wells all homered for the Bombers that afternoon.
Both teams went 5-5 in their last ten games of the regular season.
As for this series, manager Aaron Boone left Aaron Judge off the Wild Card round roster but activated Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham after both have been inactive for months and weeks at a time, respectively.
“[I’m] real confident if we play our game and pitch like we’re capable of, we got a chance to move on,” Boone said. “We got to play our best starting Tuesday.”

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman is expected to be busy this winter. While the Bronx Bombers are set to begin their playoff push after winning 93 games in 2026, the roster could certainly improve. Third base is a clear area for Cashman to target in the offseason. Catcher and center field are also positions to keep an eye on.
Nevertheless, the Yankees could soon have a massive hole at second base as well. Jazz Chisholm is set to become an unrestricted free agent after his one-year, $10.2 million deal ends. A continued partnership between the two-time All-Star and New York was previously considered a no-brainer. In fact, the Yankees were once predicted to give Chisholm a $300 million extension. This, however, now seems increasingly unlikely.
Bleacher Report’s Zach Buckley is now anticipating that New York will sign fellow second baseman Brandon Lowe this winter. The current Pittsburgh Pirates infielder is expected to be one of the top players at his position in free agency and is not expected to re-sign with his current club. According to the reporter, the Yankees should be able to land Lowe on a three-year contract.
This is not the first time that Buckley has linked the New York Yankees to Lowe. The writer previously claimed that Cashman will soon replace Chisholm with the Pirates star. Buckley even predicted that the second baseman could get at least $25 million per year in his next deal. If true, the Yankees will be rewarding the infielder with a $75 million contract in the coming months.
New York Yankees Will Face Heavy Competition to Sign Brandon Lowe
Assuming the New York Yankees sign Lowe, it would seemingly be an upgrade at the position. The Pirates infielder currently beats Chisholm in practically every offensive category. In fact, stolen bases are the only significant area where the Yankees star has the edge. Lowe, on the other hand, is slashing an impressive .260/.331/.493 in Pittsburgh this season.
He led all Major League Baseball second basemen in home runs, slugging, and OPS on the campaign as well. Lowe’s 5.4 WAR was also tops among players at his position in 2026. Overall, this particular figure was tied for 15th-best in all of baseball. In fact, the second baseman’s WAR was only slightly lower than other stars such as Junior Caminero, Randy Arozarena, and Elly De La Cruz.
The New York Yankees, however, will face tough competition in the Lowe sweepstakes. As Buckley points out, several MLB teams will want to sign the star in free agency. The Toronto Blue Jays have already been linked with a potential move for the infielder as well.
New York Set to Host Rivals in Postseason Clash
For now, the New York Yankees will focus on the 2026 playoffs. The club is set to host the Boston Red Sox in the wild card round. The two rivals will begin the five-game series in the Bronx on September 29. New York recently named Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, and Gerrit Cole as starting pitchers for the first three games. Immediately following the campaign, however, Cashman will look to free agency to strengthen his roster.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders’ season filled with highlights, memorable moments
item.dc:creator: Scott Walsh
item.description: Although they missed the playoffs, the season was a successful one for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders. Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders’ season filled with highlights, memorable moments From callups, debuts and rehab assignments to milestones and records, Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre witnessed a lot This was the final season that Scranton/Wilkes-Barre will be known
item.content:encoded:
Although they missed the playoffs, the season was a successful one for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders. They finished 78-68 overall — 41-31 in the second half — and were in contention for the postseason until the final weekend.
Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders’ season filled with highlights, memorable moments
From callups, debuts and rehab assignments to milestones and records, Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre witnessed a lot
This was the final season that Scranton/Wilkes-Barre will be known as the RailRiders; the team is rebranding next season.
“As a team, we were able to do a lot of good things and play some really good baseball for the most part,” pitcher Brendan Beck said. “It’s a bummer we came up a little short in the playoff push, but only one team can make it. We were playing meaningful baseball until the very end, so it was a good year.”
Beck, the Yankees’ No. 27 prospect according to MLB Pipeline, provided perhaps the biggest highlight of the season on June 5 at Syracuse when he combined with Carson Coleman on a no-hitter — the seventh in franchise history (third nine-inning). The right-hander was named International League Pitcher of the Year after finishing tied for second in wins with 10 and leading the league in ERA (2.93), strikeouts (151), innings (135.1), WHIP (1.06), and opponents’ batting average (.210). His strikeout total ranks fourth in franchise single-season history and his ERA ranks fifth.
On May 7, Beck made his major-league debut at Yankee Stadium against the Texas Rangers. Other RailRiders who got the call and made their major league debuts included Elmer Rodriguez (April 29), Spencer Jones (May 8), George Lombard Jr. (Aug. 4), Bradley Hanner (Aug. 14) and Alexander Cornielle (Sept. 25).
Rodriguez joined Beck on the International League All-Star team. The right-hander, who is the Yankees’ No. 2 prospect, went 8-4 with the RailRiders with a 2.45 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 106.1 innings.
Not only did the RailRiders have players who went up, but they also had a number of players come down, such as Jasson Dominguez, Anthony Volpe, and J.C. Escarra. Several Yankees players also did rehab assignments — pitchers Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon, catcher Austin Wells, and outfielder Cody Bellinger.
“There’s been more movement on this team, more back and forth turnover with position players and pitchers than any team I’ve been on,” manager Shelley Duncan said. “Had a lot of guys come down from the big leagues with a tough mindset and they really gave themselves to the team. A lot of guys here with deep, strong individual aspirations and they poured themselves into the team. I’ve seen us go through stretches where things were bleak and they don’t give up hope or shut it down. They fight through it. I’ve seen players grow, I’ve seen some guys have some unbelievable years. I’ve seen some guys make some big career jumps. There’s a lot this season.”
Besides Beck, several other RailRiders ranked among the International League leaders. Yanquiel Fernandez tied for third in home runs with 27, ranked third in RBIs with 87, and tied for ninth in hits with 126. Oswaldo Cabrera tied for fifth in hits with 134 and was 10th in batting at .288 (134 for 466).
Duke Ellis finished second in the league in stolen bases with 60, one behind Worcester’s Braiden Ward. Ellis set the franchise single-season record for steals, breaking the mark of 44 set by the Red Barons’ Tommy Barrett in 1989. He also became the franchise’s career leader in steals with 102, surpassing the record of 82 held by the Red Barons’ Nick Punto. Ellis also ended the season with a 15-game hitting streak and a 20-game on-base streak.
Another highlight was a season-high eight-game winning streak from July 26 to Aug. 4, including a six-game series sweep in Iowa against the Chicago Cubs’ Triple-A affiliate. It was the first time since 1990 that a Scranton/Wilkes-Barre team visited Iowa.
That winning streak gave the RailRiders a 23-9 record in the second half, good for first place in the standings by one game over the Durham Bulls and two over the Indianapolis Indians. However, they lost their next four games to Rochester at PNC Field by a combined 40-11 and that was the turning point for the RailRiders. Interestingly, that also was the turning point for the Red Wings and as they went 27-14 the rest of the way to win the second-half title, then capture the league championship over the first-half champion Memphis Redbirds. Rochester lost to the Pacific Coast League champion Oklahoma City Comets in 10 innings, 5-3, in the Triple-A National Championship Game in Las Vegas.
“It’s really a shame we were not in the playoffs,” relief pitcher Eric Reyzelman said. “I feel if this team got a chance to play in there, we would have been the last team coming out of Vegas. It’s tough the way it ended, but we played hard until the last second.”
While winning a championship would have been a storybook ending to the RailRiders era, it was still an exciting, memorable season.

item.title: [Newsday] Yankees vs. Red Sox: The AL Wild Card Series blog
item.description: The Yankees and Red Sox renew their long-standing rivalry by facing each other in the AL Wild Card Series. Look who's taking BP for the Yanks Look who's taking BP for the Yankees. (via @DPLennon) pic.twitter.com/amwk8zvMUw — Newsday Sports (@NewsdaySports) September 28, 2026 Rizzo: Judge is 'a game-changer' — if he's healthy The status of Aaron Judge (right calf strain) remains in doubt ahead of the start of the AL Wild Card Series on Tuesday. But his former teammate Anthony Rizzo, who will be t
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees and Red Sox renew their long-standing rivalry by facing each other in the AL Wild Card Series.
Look who's taking BP for the Yanks
Look who's taking BP for the Yankees. (via @DPLennon) pic.twitter.com/amwk8zvMUw
— Newsday Sports (@NewsdaySports) September 28, 2026
Rizzo: Judge is 'a game-changer' — if he's healthy
The status of Aaron Judge (right calf strain) remains in doubt ahead of the start of the AL Wild Card Series on Tuesday.
But his former teammate Anthony Rizzo, who will be the "Inside the Pitch" analyst on NBC Sports’ broadcast of the Yankees’ three-game series vs. the Red Sox, has no doubt that Judge will be impactful if he finds his way on the roster.
“I think he could be a big factor if he's on the roster, if he's healthy enough to be on the roster,” Rizzo said Monday afternoon on an NBC Sports conference call previewing the Wild Card Series. “I know he wants to be in there. It's Yankees-Red Sox. This is a massive rivalry. You cannot take any playoff game for granted, right? You don't know when you're going to be back. But if he's in the lineup, I expect him to be a huge factor.
“Aaron Judge standing in the batter's box is Aaron Judge standing in the batter's box. It doesn't matter if he's on one leg. It doesn't matter if he has one arm. He is a threat, and he will be respected by every pitcher that's facing him.”
Rizzo has experience wearing pinstripes and facing Boston in the postseason. The Red Sox defeated the Yankees, 6-2, in the 2021 AL Wild Card Game – a game in which Rizzo hit a solo homer.
As an “Inside the Pitch” analyst, Rizzo will be offering insight from the batter’s perspective and will be located outside the broadcast booth, likely near the dugouts.
“Hopefully for the game [Judge is] in there, and hopefully he's at whatever the full strength he's at and can stay healthy through the longevity of these playoffs,” Rizzo added. “But it's going to be, I mean, him being in there will be a game-changer, in my opinion.”
Cam Schlittler and his 'receipts'
Cam Schlittler drew some of his motivation before last season's dominant performance in the deciding third game of the AL Wild Card series against Boston from social media, talking afterward about some of the uglier posts from Red Sox fans that involved threats against his family.
Schlittler, on the eve of his start in Game 1 of this best-of-three series, indicated he has done the same in advance of Tuesday night.
“I wouldn't say I'm always on my phone looking for that stuff. At the same time, I don't really live under a rock as well,” Schlittler said Monday afternoon before the Yankees worked out at the Stadium. “Found ways to use that to my advantage. I think I'm good at keeping receipts. At the end of the day, I'm locked into going in there tomorrow and doing my job.”
So, a reporter asked, does Schlittler already have a “receipt” or two in tow for Tuesday night?
“Again, I don't live under a rock,” the 25-year-old righthander said. “I mean, there's always going to be motivation, fuel. At the same time, I'm not too worried about any of that. I feel like I did a good job proving that last year, and I expect to go out there tomorrow and do the same thing."
Is it safe to say that you’ve collected a few receipts in advance of the start?
“Close to the same question, but again,” Schlittler, smiling widely, said to laughter from the assembled reporters. “Yeah, we'll see. Again, my mind's on tomorrow and the game. I don't (have) to look too far to motivate myself, and I trust the guys in this locker room to go out there and compete to their best ability.”
Schlittler has done that through the season, going 14-6 with a league-low 1.95 ERA. He was especially tough on the Red Sox, going 2-1 with a 0.74 ERA in four starts.
"It's natural adrenaline. I expect it to be loud. It's going to be an electric experience."

Cam Schlittler talks about taking the mound in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series: pic.twitter.com/jszrTxirv1
From Chipotle to Yankee Stadium, what a year for Spencer Jones
On the eve of his first Yankees-Red Sox October showdown, Spencer Jones was asked where he was a year ago when the two teams clashed in the Wild Card Series.
“I was driving home from Scranton,” Jones said Monday, referring to the Yankees’ Triple-A outpost. “I was watching it on my iPad, my girlfriend and I, and we watched Cam pitch Game 3. So that was my experience in the postseason last year.”
Jones quickly pointed out that both he and his girlfriend were taking turns driving, so whoever was behind the wheel had their eyes primarily on the road.
“I remember we stopped at Chipotle and watched a couple of innings,” Jones said.
Jones wrapped up a solid rookie season, hitting .245 with 11 homers, 40 RBIs and a .742 OPS in 86 games. Perhaps most impressive, Jones showed that he wasn’t just a platoon player, batting .389 (21-for-54) with a 1.107 OPS against lefthanders.
“I think it comes down to the work that we’ve done behind the scenes in the cages,” Jones said. “The stuff that we talk about in meetings, conversations I have with other hitters. We have a lot of really good lefthanded hitters on this team and they’ve been able to help me refine my approach - just kind of go up there and be confident in what I got to do.”
Aaron Judge is in it for the long haul this postseason
Aaron Judge, out with a right calf strain, all but guaranteed to Yankees fans Monday they will see him at some point this postseason.
And if not in the upcoming wild-card round – something the three-time AL MVP still isn’t ruling out – then after. Which, in essence, was the club's captain stating unequivocably his belief the Yankees will be moving on to the ALDS.
“I think the most important thing is just making sure I’m healthy and ready to go for this long stretch, because we’ve got another month of baseball to play,” Judge said before heading out to the Yankee Stadium field to partake in a simulated game. “So I want to be ready for the long run we’re going to go on here for this next month. We’re all going to be smart, but I think they all know I want to be out there, especially in the first game.”
Judge missed three months of the season with a right rib fracture and appeared in all of seven games after his return on Sept. 8 before landing back on the IL on Sept. 19 with the calf strain.
The Yankees played reasonably well without Judge, unlike in past seasons when he’s missed extended time, going 45-39 while he recovered from the rib injury.
During that time, the Yankees brought up two of their heralded prospects, Spencer Jones and George Lombard Jr., both of whom have, at least in the early going of their respective big-league careers, appeared to gain their footing at the sport’s highest level.
“That’s definitely the goal,” Judge said of returning. “I’m busting my butt in the back room to try to do everything I can to get ready and be prepared and be a productive player for the team…no matter what happens this first series, we’ve got a great ballclub. You know, I’ve been out for most of the year, and this team’s picked up the slack…the boys are going to be fine no matter what. But I’d love to be out there in the trenches with them.”
Jazz or Volpe at 2B? 'The platoon stuff is in play'
Last year, a visibly upset Jazz Chisholm Jr. was benched for Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, as manager Aaron Boone opted to go with the rigthy-hitting Amed Rosario against Red Sox ace Garrett Crochet.
On Tuesday, the Yankees will be facing another hard-throwing lefthander, rookie Payton Tolle, and Chisholm said before Monday’s workout that he hadn’t spoken with Boone about the lineup plans for the opener.
“We haven’t had that talk yet,” Chisholm said at his locker. “But I feel like with Boonie, he will come up to me and let me know what’s going on.”
Chisholm batted .218 with a .650 OPS vs. lefties this season, and is 1-for-5 with a home run and two strikeouts against Tolle. Boone could go with Anthony Volpe as a righty option for second base, and the manager said he’s open to the idea of a platoon at the position.
“It’s one of those things I’m considering,” Boone said. “Volpe’s very much in play. The platoon stuff is in play there. Obviously Jazz is just coming back from the thumb (sprain). He was able to get a couple games in. Would have liked another one or two, but the weather didn’t really cooperate this weekend. So Anthony’s put himself very much in the mix to be a part of the equation.”
Chisholm said he expects to be starting Game 1 but understands Boone’s matchup strategy, if that’s the way this plays out.
“It’s playoff baseball, so it’s different,” Chisholm said.
Still, the pending free agent believes in riding with your best players, no matter the time of year.
“That’s what I grew up watching and seeing, you know what I mean?” Chisholm said. “It’s always been that.”
Aaron Boone on Aaron Judge's health
Aaron Boone was asked how realistic it is to have Aaron Judge play right field at this point:

"I don't know. We'll continue to evaluate and I'll listen to trainers and medical and see where we're at." pic.twitter.com/2Hvud0RJ74
Aaron Boone says that Aaron Judge did some hitting insde yesterday and he believes Judge will be part of the live BP today:

"He's making progress. We'll continue to see where he's at." pic.twitter.com/qOjDytyix9
'This guy's a pretty darn good pitcher'
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy, who managed Boston’s Triple-A affiliate Worcester from 2022 until taking over for the fired Alex Cora in late April, recalled seeing the Yankees' Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler a couple of years ago when the pitcher was with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre.
“My first impression was, this guy’s a pretty darn good pitcher,” Tracy said Monday afternoon.
Schlittler, the presumed AL Cy Young Award winner after going 14-6 with a league-low 1.95 ERA, went 2-1 with a 0.74 ERA in four starts against the Red Sox. All of that on the heels of his historic Game 3 performance against the Red Sox in last year’s wild-card round when he struck out 12 over eight scoreless innings in a 4-0 victory.
“For me, regardless of who you’re facing, your job is grind at-bats, grind at-bats,” Tracy said. “And if it’s an out and you’re able to see six pitches, fine. If it’s a line out, fine. If it’s finding a way to get two people on base, fine. And I don’t think that changes, regardless of who you face. That always plays, right? I just think it becomes even more prevalent when you’re facing really good pitching.”
Chad Tracy recalls facing Cam Schlittler in the minor leagues

"My first impression was this guy's a pretty darn good pitcher. My impression hasn't changed since then" pic.twitter.com/yhGgA6aqcd
Willson Contreras expected to be ready for Game 1
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy sounded confident that Willson Contreras, arguably the team's MVP this season, will be a full-go for Tuesday night's Game 1. The All-Star first baseman was dealing with a bruised right hand and finally played Sunday after missing the previous 10 days with the injury.
"You're always monitoring," Tracy said. "As far as this time of year, players are banged up. The adrenaline will kick in tomorrow and guys tend to go. But he's in a good spot ... I think he's ready to go."
Working around the weather
The Yankees planned today's workout time for 3:15 p.m. in the hope that the remnants from the nor'easter would be finished in the Bronx by then.
As for the Red Sox, they had two choices -- either before the Yankees or after -- and they decided to go in the earlier slot. As of now, the tarp is coming off the field, but it's unclear if it will be ready in time for Boston. Also, the Red Sox had Sunday's Game 162 vs. the Cubs moved to Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, so their travel itinerary became a bit more complicated at the last minute.
"If we were able to get on the field, great," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. "If not, we did have a game yesterday, did a bunch of stuff yesterday and then played. Based on our travel, we left it up to (the players) what they they wanted to do and this is what they preferred."
Yankees-Red Sox ticket prices on the secondary market
Looking to head to the Bronx for the American League Wild Card Series between the Yankees and the Red Sox?
Here’s what ticket prices look like for each of the three games, according to TickPick as of noon Monday.
Game 1, Tuesday, 8 p.m.
Get-in price: $108
Average ticket cost: $360
Game 2, Wednesday, 8 p.m.
Get-in price: $113
Average ticket cost: $400
Game 3 (if necessary), Thursday, 8 p.m.
Get-in price: $112
Average ticket cost: $401
Red Sox set pitching rotation for series
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy announced early Monday afternoon that power lefty Payton Tolle will start Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series, with former Yankee Sonny Gray set for Game 2. If a Game 3 is necessary, it will be Ranger Suarez.
Tolle, 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA in 26 starts this season, went 1-0 with a 0.69 ERA in two starts against the Yankees.
Gray, an AL Cy Young Award candidate, went 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA in 29 starts. He faced the Yankees twice, going 1-0 with a 1.98 ERA.
Suarez went 8-5 with a 3.22 ERA in 28 starts, including 0-6 with a 6.06 ERA in three starts against the Yankees.
The Red Sox were scheduled to work out on the Yankee Stadium field at 1 p.m. Monday but, as of 12:55 p.m., it was still raining in The Bronx and the tarp was on the field.
Yankees and Red Sox meet again in playoffs
The Yankees and Red Sox will square off in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series a second straight season, with Game 1 scheduled for 8 p.m. Tuesday night at the Stadium.
Game 2 is Wednesday night with Game 3, if necessary, Thursday night.
All games will be played at the Stadium.
It is the first time the long-time rivals have met in back-to-back postseasons since the epic ALCS battles of 2003 and 2004.
The Yankees won in ’03, winning the pennant in a memorable Game 7 at old Yankee Stadium on a walk-off homer by current manager Aaron Boone. That game brought an end to Grady Little’s managerial tenure in Boston and his replacement, Terry Francona, would become a long-time tormentor of the Yankees. That started a year later in the ALCS when the Red Sox became the first, and still only, Major League Baseball club in history to come back from a three-games-to-none deficit to win a series.
Both the Yankees and Red Sox are scheduled to work out this afternoon in The Bronx, weather permitting.
The Red Sox flew to New York late Sunday night from Tampa, Florida. Because of the nor’easter that hammered the East Coast over the weekend, the Red Sox's regular season-finale against the Cubs was moved, as a precautionary move, to Tropicana Field, home of the Rays.
The Red Sox, who have not yet announced their Game 1 starter but will early this afternoon, are scheduled to work out at 1 p.m. The Yankees, who announced Cam Schlittler as their Game 1 starter Sunday afternoon, are scheduled to work out at 3:15 p.m.
Your radio and TV choices for Yankees vs. Red Sox
The Yankees-Red Sox series will be broadcast on NBC and streamed on Peacock in NBC's first season as the TV carrier for all four Wild-Card series.
All season, NBC has used its own play-by-play announcers (with Jason Benetti as the No. 1) and analysts from each team for its MLB slate.
Benetti will call the Yankees-Red Sox series with Joe Girardi moving from the YES booth to the NBC booth as the Yankees-related analyst. The Red Sox will be represented by NESN's Lou Merloni. Former Yankees first baseman Anthony Rizzo will be the "Inside the Pitch" analyst, giving the hitter's perspective usually from a spot near one of the dugouts. Rizzo also will join Bob Costas from Yankee Stadium for NBC's pregame show.
On the radio side, Dave Sims and Suzyn Waldman will call the games as usual for WFAN. A new wrinkle for this series is Yankees TV play-by-play man on Michael Kay will be doing the national radio broadcast for ESPN. It will be heard locally on 1050 AM, with Game 2 also on 880. Kay will be joined by analysts Eduardo Perez and Tim Kurkjian.
The Yankees-Red Sox playoff history
The rivalry between the Yankees and Red Sox began more than 100 years ago. And since MLB first added wild cards to its postseason format in 1995, the Yankees and Red Sox have met in the playoffs six times before this year's Wild-Card best-of-three series.
Here's how they went:
1999: Yankees win the ALCS, 4-1
Game 3 featured a legendary matchup of pitchers in Roger Clemens vs. Pedro Martinez. The Red Sox handled their business in that game, but the Yankees took care of the series in relatively smooth fashion. Orlando "El Duque" Hernandez was the ALCS MVP with two impressive starts, including the win in Game 5.
2003: Yankees win the ALCS, 4–3
Perhaps the pinnacle of the Yankees-Red Sox rivalry over the last few generations of fans, at least from a New York point of view. This series had it all: bench-clearing brouhahas, players tossing coaches to the ground, players hopping outfield fences and fighting with the grounds crew. And that was just Game 3! Eventually, it got to a Game 7 at Yankee Stadium, a night that included three innings of scoreless relief by both Mike Mussina and Mariano Rivera, an eighth-inning rally against Pedro Martinez, and, of course, Aaron "Bleeping" Boone's walkoff homer in the bottom of the 11th inning to send the Yankees to the World Series.
2004: Red Sox win the ALCS, 4-3
The Yankees led this series, 3-0, before Boston made MLB history by becoming the first (and still the only) team to come back and win a postseason series after dropping the first three games. The Red Sox won the World Series that season, ending an 86-year drought and effectively ending "The Curse of the Bambino."
2018: Red Sox win ALDS, 3–1
Masahiro Tanaka had the lone win for the Yankees in Game 2. But Game 3 saw the Yankees suffer their worst postseason loss in franchise history, a 16-1 drubbing at home.
2021: Red Sox win AL Wild-Card game, 1-0
The Wild-Card round was still just a single game playoff, and the Red Sox took a 2-0 lead in the first inning when Xander Bogaerts hit a two-run homer off Gerrit Cole. The Red Sox never looked back.
2025: Yankees win AL Wild-Card series, 2-1
Cam Schlittler entered the chat. The Massachusetts-born and raised pitcher struck out 12 over eight innings in the Yankees' 4-0 win in Game 3 to beat his hometown team.
Pitching matchups for Yankees-Red Sox series
The Red Sox said they will wait until Monday to announce their pitching rotation for the three-game Wild-Card series with the Yankees.
The Yankees, however, released their rotation on Sunday.
Game 1: Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA)
Game 2: Max Fried (5-5, 2.80)
Game 3 (if necessary): Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61)
Yankees vs. Red Sox wild-card schedule
All games in this best-of-three AL Wild-Card series will be played at Yankee Stadium and broadcast on NBC and its Peacock streaming platform.
Game 1: Tuesday, Sept. 29, 8 p.m.
Game 2: Wednesday, Sept. 30, 8 p.m.
Game 3 (if necessary): Thursday, Oct. 1, TBD
The winning team will face the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS starting on Saturday, Oct. 3. That series will be shown on TBS and HBO Max.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees September Approval Poll: Brian Cashman
item.dc:creator: Estevão Maximo
item.description: The thing about chasing an object is that if it matches your speed, there is really nothing you can do. The New York Yankees learned this hard lesson down the stretch when any goals they had of running down the Rays to at least make it a competitive fight down the stretch fell flat — not because the Yankees underwhelmed in the final month of the season. In fact, one could hardly ask for more out of this team given the obstacles it had to face as the Rays left nothing to chance. Despite winning 1
item.content:encoded:
The thing about chasing an object is that if it matches your speed, there is really nothing you can do. The New York Yankees learned this hard lesson down the stretch when any goals they had of running down the Rays to at least make it a competitive fight down the stretch fell flat — not because the Yankees underwhelmed in the final month of the season. In fact, one could hardly ask for more out of this team given the obstacles it had to face as the Rays left nothing to chance. Despite winning 15 of 23 games in September, the Yankees couldn't gain a game on the Rays, who won 16 of 24 to wrap up their season.
What looked like the likeliest scenario for quite some time now, given the state of the other two divisions in the American League, has come to pass. The Yankees, who are the second-best team in the AL, will have to go through the most difficult of schedules to make it out of their league for the second time in the past three seasons. A three-game Wild Card round against the feisty Boston Red Sox and all the potential pitfalls a short series can bring await—one with a feeling of déjà vu, happening for the second straight season. Then, if they make it out, it's a date with the Rays while the AL Central and AL West clubs battle it out on the inferior side of the bracket.
It hasn't been the smoothest ride to get to this point, and based on how Brian Cashman has polled all year long, it's safe to say expectations were not met — even if there are obvious caveats beyond his control as to why the Yankees are exactly where they are. Early in the season, when Cashman polled at 41 percent, the Yankees were battling with the Rays for the AL East title — but if you polled most fans, you would've been hard-pressed to find many who bought the Rays as a 99-win team. Frankly, there are probably those who, even now, don't buy them at that level even now, but that's an entirely separate conversation to have in the analysis of the gap between these two clubs, particularly at full strength. Cashman's approval rating nosedived as did the Yankees' chances of winning this division, partially due to questionable moves but overwhelmingly due to absences that all the money in the world couldn't plan for.
For three months between June and August, the Yankees put up a wRC+ below league average, clearly struggling in the absence of the best hitter in the sport. The deadline acquisition of Luis Garcia Jr. in particular gave the offense a boost as he delivered an .842 OPS in August — even that wasn't enough to take the team's line over 100, coming in with a 96 wRC+ for the month.
In September, though, the offense came through with a 104 wRC+ that may not seem like much, but with this team's rotation, it's how you go about winning 15 of 23 games. All of this after starting off the month with the bad news of yet another Trent Grisham hamstring injury, this one keeping him out for the rest of the regular season. Spencer Jones continues to defy the laws of what can be described as sensible production coming with obscene strikeout rates, with a 110 wRC+ on the month despite a strikeout rate above 38 percent.
While Aaron Judge's brief return before getting injured again helps, this September improvement boils down primarily to the work of Ben Rice, who, after a disappointing summer — given the high bar he set for himself — came alive in a big way. Still, if you're wondering about the changes in impact from Rice with and without a fully stocked lineup, the Yankees first baseman delivered 21 RBI with seven homers in 24 games in May. The same Rice then hit six homers in 22 games this past month and only drove in 11. Those 11 RBI did not lead the team, with the distinction left to George Lombard Jr., who drove in 16 with five homers, providing more power than he had in the previous month. Back to the deadline acquisitions, though, as Garcia cooled off, Heliot Ramos finally showed up, proving a worthy presence in the lineup, specifically against left-handed pitchers.
It was business as usual for this ultra-talented staff, with Cam Schlittler wrapping up a likely Cy Young campaign with yet another sub-2.00 ERA month. Carlos Rodón was nearly as dominant as Schlittler, with both kind of showing up Max Fried, who had a solid September, and, lastly, Will Warren impressing; the only one who had more than his fair share of issues was Gerrit Cole. But looking forward to the Wild Card round in which he'll start the third game, if needed, Cole impressed in his final regular-season start against the Rays.
About the Wild Card round, the Yankees already announced their starters versus Boston, with Schlittler going in game 1, followed by Fried and lastly Cole. While Boston hasn't officially announced their starters, expectations are that Sonny Gray, the AL leader in wins this season with 18, will take the ball for Game 1 and likely be followed by left-hander Payton Tolle.
When it comes to transactions, not a lot stood out. With a plethora of utility options, the Yankees chose to designate Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment when they had to open up a 40-man spot for Clarke Schmidt. Cabrera was picked up by the Reds and was one of two players to leave the Yankees this month, alongside righty Chase Hampton — picked up by the Nats (and recently discarded) after being DFA'd early in the month. Hampton didn't appear in the bigs for the Yankees.
It's a simple yet loaded question whether you approve of Cashman's job in September, depending on how much emphasis you want to give to certain merits and demerits in how the Yankees have been managed this season. In many ways, the déjà vu doesn't come strictly from a playoff series against the Red Sox. It's more so from yet another second-place finish in the AL East against a team widely regarded as inferior to the Yankees before the start of the season.
So with the regular season officially over and the playoffs immediately ahead, do you approve of Brian Cashman? As always, there's a lot to factor into a "yes" or a "no," and you might feel like your answer is more of a soft "yes" or "no" than a stamp of approval or a sharp rebuke. However, the binary question is the best way to get a direct read on fans' thoughts.
Vote in the poll below and let us know! We'll revisit the results at the end of October.
Note: This is the same poll that is currently appearing on the Feed, so if you've voted there, that should already be counted.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Predicting the Yankees' Wild Card Series playoff roster as chaotic decisions hang in the balance
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: The New York Yankees' season has left them with a unique playoff roster-building challenge that may not make it to the next CBA. How do you load up a roster aimed at taking advantage of the Boston Red Sox's weaknesses (left-handed pitching, especially if they're without Willson Contreras) without using too many pitchers? How do you avoid wasting roster spots that could've been nabbed by some of the game's biggest offensive stars? This isn't what I believe the Yankees should do. It's what I belie
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees' season has left them with a unique playoff roster-building challenge that may not make it to the next CBA. How do you load up a roster aimed at taking advantage of the Boston Red Sox's weaknesses (left-handed pitching, especially if they're without Willson Contreras) without using too many pitchers? How do you avoid wasting roster spots that could've been nabbed by some of the game's biggest offensive stars?
This isn't what I believe the Yankees should do. It's what I believe they will do. This is all to say I've been potentially hooked and swindled by some of their pre-series bluster, but ... I really do believe they believe, like Seal once said, they're never gonna survive unless they get a little crazy,
Aaron Boone has said that the Yankees will not carry 12 pitchers in the opening round, and may not even carry 11. So, for the sake of the exercise, how do we get to a 26-man roster with only 10 pitchers?
Projecting a Yankees playoff roster with only 10 pitchers for the Wild Card Series vs. Red Sox
Yankees Rotation: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole
The Yankees did it. They kept things close to the vest, then went with their strongest starter in first position.
When I believed they were about to choose Fried for Game 1, I wrote an extended monologue justifying the choice, calling it "not quite as silly a gambit as Deivi Garcia/JA Happ". After all, strong hints were wafting from the Yankees' clubhouse that they intended to stay on turn and start Max Fried, he of the 1.93 career ERA against the Red Sox and 11 2/3 innings with a single earned run allowed against them this year, so I had to justify it. The fact that they were reticent to go to Schlittler on anything less than a day's extra rest hinted to me that they had some workload concerns, and were trying to sell the choice in a different way. Carlos Rodón probably should get a start, but, again ... good problems. Lot of talent. He'll be available to caddy.
Cole in a potential win-or-go-home game scares me, but the Yankees don't have a single bad option here. Thankfully, they came to their senses to start things off and didn't play with their food. Fried still looks like a pretty excellent Game 2 choice for all the reasons mentioned above.
Yankees Bullpen (again, we're trying to get by with only seven names): Carlos Rodón, Will Warren, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, David Bednar, John Schreiber, Tim Hill
Clarke Schmidt was a core option until the season's final week; he'll end the year with less than one inning pitched in his frenzied comeback bid. Aaron Boone said that, while Ryan Weathers hit 96 in his latest live bullpen session, he might not be an option for this round. He then waffled on that Sunday. We'll take him at his initial word in this projection.
There isn't much debate here, given our limitations, besides, "Is Rodón worth carrying?" and, "Michael Fulmer vs. Tim Hill vs. Ryan Yarbrough". If the Yankees add an 11th pitcher, our guess is Fulmer for a righty look. Hill could be left out for Yarbrough. It's very much on the table.
Yankees Lineup and Bench: Austin Wells, Ali Sanchez, Ben Rice, Paul Goldschmidt, Jazz Chisholm Jr., George Lombard Jr., Jose Caballero, Spencer Jones, Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, Luis Garcia Jr., Trent Grisham, Anthony Volpe, Ryan McMahon, Giancarlo Stanton, Aaron Judge
Overloaded? Absolutely. But when you need a home run in the later innings, and both Stanton and Judge tell you they're available, who are you leaving off? Would you rather have Judge active and simmering behind the scenes, or Michael Fulmer? Ryan McMahon may very well have been the final addition here, but he's also likely to start Game 2, after all that consternation, with Fried on the bump.
Stanton and Judge have made projecting a realistic roster somewhat impossible. Both could arrive on Tuesday begging for an at-bat or two. Judge could arrive and claim he's fully healthy, ready to start in right. The Yankees have opted for theatricality plenty this season, whether it be Fried returning out of the shadows against Pittsburgh or Cole staying in for Max Muncy. This would be another example.
Or it might be all bluster, and Fulmer and Yarbs can take the bump instead of the modern-day Mantle and Maris. And what if Grisham's not ready? This leaves Amed Rosario on the outside looking in. He, too, could realistically start Game 1 against Payton Tolle.
For the first time in quite a while, the Yankees have plenty up for grabs when the roster graphic drops. This is our estimation in which they push the limits of health and viability, but they hold the cards, and they've pledged to get weird. So we did, too.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Yankees’ Carlos Rodon Lands Disappointing News Before Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Jake Rogers
item.description: The New York Yankees will open the American League Wild Card Series without Carlos Rodón on the mound as a starter, a decision that lands as disappointing news for the left-hander after a strong late-season stretch. Manager Aaron Boone confirmed the rotation Sunday after rain washed out the club’s regular-season finale against the Baltimore Orioles. Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 on Tuesday night against the Boston Red Sox at Yankee Stadium. Max Fried is lined up for Game 2. Gerrit Cole would
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will open the American League Wild Card Series without Carlos Rodón on the mound as a starter, a decision that lands as disappointing news for the left-hander after a strong late-season stretch.
Manager Aaron Boone confirmed the rotation Sunday after rain washed out the club’s regular-season finale against the Baltimore Orioles. Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 on Tuesday night against the Boston Red Sox at Yankee Stadium. Max Fried is lined up for Game 2. Gerrit Cole would pitch Game 3 if the series goes the distance.
That alignment leaves Rodón without a start in the best-of-three matchup. For a pitcher who has looked sharp since returning from injury, the news is a setback even if the team still plans to keep him on the roster.
Rodón finished the regular season 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA across 16 starts. Over his last seven outings he posted a 1.89 ERA, giving the Yankees a fourth starter performing at a high level just as October began.
Boone said he expects to have Carlos Rodon on the roster to pitch out of the bullpen in the Wild Card series. Will Warren will also move to relief duty for the short series.
The arrangement is practical. A best-of-three format only requires three starters, and the Yankees have four quality arms. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, earned the opener. Fried and Cole follow. Rodón becomes the odd man out for now.
That does not erase the disappointment. Starters typically want the ball in October, not a relief role after months of building toward a postseason start. Rodón has dealt with elbow issues this year, including surgery last offseason and a midsummer inflammation stint, yet he delivered when he returned.
Boone has described the group’s depth as the club’s greatest strength.
“It’s clearly our greatest strength this year and we haven’t had it all together at different times obviously, but I do feel like all four of those guys are throwing the ball incredibly well right now at the right time,” Boone said.
The Yankees still value that depth. If they advance past Boston, the next series would be best-of-five. In that case Rodón would be a strong candidate to return to the rotation, possibly as early as Game 1 or Game 4 of an AL Division Series.
For this first round, though, his assignment is different. The bullpen role could include multiple innings if a starter exits early or a game tightens late. It is useful work, but it is not the same as lining up for a start against a rival the Yankees just faced in last year’s Wild Card round.
Boston presents a familiar test. The Red Sox and Yankees meet again in the Bronx after New York eliminated them a year ago. Schlittler already has a strong playoff history against them. The rest of the staff will be asked to follow.
Rodón’s recent form made the choice harder, not easier. A 1.89 ERA over seven starts is the kind of run that usually locks in a postseason start. Instead, the short series and the presence of Schlittler, Fried and Cole pushed him to the side.
The Yankees have not framed the move as a demotion. Boone has said Rodón remains very much in the conversation. Still, conversation is not the same as a Game 1, 2 or 3 assignment.
Playoff baseball often rewards flexibility. A left-hander with Rodón’s stuff could help bridge innings or face a key stretch of Boston’s lineup. That value is real. It does not change the fact that he will watch the first two games from a different vantage point than he likely hoped.
If New York wins the series quickly, Cole might even be held for the next round and Rodón’s path back to starting could open sooner. If it goes three games, Cole takes the mound and Rodón stays in reserve.
Either way, the initial announcement is clear. Rodón will not start in the Wild Card Series. For a pitcher who finished the year pitching well, that is the disappointing part of Sunday’s news.
The focus now shifts to Tuesday. Schlittler takes the ball first. Fried and Cole wait behind him. Rodón waits in the bullpen, ready if needed, and hoping the series lasts long enough — or the next series arrives soon enough — for another chance to start.

Aaron Boone had nothing but good options to open the wild-card series Tuesday night. In the end, he went with his best — and the one that would cause the least second-guessing and noise. item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — The regular-season finale between the Baltimore Orioles and New York Yankees on Sunday was canceled because of sustained rain.
New York will host Boston in an AL Wild Card Series starting Tuesday. Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 on Tuesday, followed by Max Fried and Gerrit Cole.
Aaron Judge appears doubtful for the Wild Card Series because of a calf injury. As of Sunday, Judge’s only activity has been plyometric exercises and running on the treadmill.
The Yankees finished 93-67. They were 94-67 in each of the prior two seasons and no team has finished with the same record in three straight seasons, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Baltimore finished 79-82 under first-year manager Craig Albernaz, up from 75-87 last year. The Orioles have had consecutive losing seasons after winning 275 games from 2022-24.
The Yankees drew drew 3,297,154 for 79 home dates, down from 3,392,659 in 80 dates last year. They had 12 home sellouts, a drop from 20 last season.
New York never announced its lineup, and the game was canceled about three hours after the scheduled 1:05 p.m. EDT start. This marked the first time since 2002 the Yankees didn't play all 162 games in a non-shortened season.

item.title: [MLB.com] Yanks turn to Cy favorite Schlittler to start G1 of Wild Card Series
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch

Gerrit Cole would start Game 3, if necessary. “Who wouldn’t want to start the first game?” Schlittler said earlier this
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The Yankees’ braintrust spent days debating their rotation in the American League Wild Card Series, only to arrive at a logical conclusion: Just hand the ball to the guy who’s about to win the AL Cy Young Award.
Cam Schlittler will face the Red Sox in Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series on Tuesday at 8 p.m. ET, the team announced, to be followed by Max Fried in Game 2. Gerrit Cole would start Game 3, if necessary.
“Who wouldn’t want to start the first game?” Schlittler said earlier this week. “I feel like this whole pitching staff kind of deserves it. We’re all competitors.”
Fried and Schlittler both tossed side sessions before Sunday's rainout at Yankee Stadium, and manager Aaron Boone said he would wait to announce his plans until both hurlers came through without incident.
Asked how Schlittler took the news, Boone replied: “He was half asleep on the training table.”
“He’ll be ready to go,” Boone added. “We talked a little bit about it a couple of days ago, having not made my decision yet. But he’s excited. He wants the ball, and he’s ready to go.”
The Yankees have been keeping close tabs on Schlittler’s workload. He’s coming off a 33-start campaign in which he posted a 14-6 record and 1.95 ERA in a career-high 193 2/3 innings.
Pitching coach Matt Blake said earlier this week that while Schlittler has “earned the right to pitch Game 1,” the righty’s health was among the items the team would consider.
Additionally, Blake noted that Schlittler has pitched on his regular day for three consecutive turns. The Yankees held Schlittler to 70 pitches in that start against Tampa Bay.
“Cam is going to win the Cy Young Award and has been the best pitcher in the league,” Boone said. “It was just working through, do we want him in a Game 2 scenario with a chance to move on and slam the door, or if your back is against the wall?
“ … It was something we debated. Different people had different stances on it. I kind of considered both things, but ultimately decided this was the way I wanted to go.”
Ultimately, common sense prevailed. Schlittler’s 1.95 ERA is the Yankees’ lowest since Ron Guidry’s 1.74 mark in 1978, and he’s in line to become the seventh Yankee to win the Cy Young Award and the first since Cole in 2023.
“He’s a student of the game,” Blake said. “He understands who he’s facing and which [pitch] shapes are going to work better to hitters. I think that’s something he’s learned a lot about as the years have gone on.”
Neck and neck with the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease in the Cy Young conversation for much of the season, Schlittler separated himself with a strong finish. He pitched to a 1.17 ERA (10 runs, seven earned) over his final nine starts, spanning 54 innings.
“He just doubled down on what we saw last year,” Blake said. “The fact that he’s held velo the way he has, the fact that he’s thrown probably more strikes than he did in July and August – it’s a testament to the work that he put in over the course of 30-plus starts to put himself in this spot.”
Of course, Schlittler knows what a playoff start in the Bronx should feel like.
“The environment, it’s electric,” Schlittler said. “Being home is important. To be in front of these fans, it’s going to be special.”

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 of the New York Yankees’ Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night and be followed in the rotation by Max Fried and Gerrit Cole in the best-of-three matchup.
New York made the announcement Sunday, the last day of the regular season.
Schlittler struck out 12 over eight innings in the Yankees’ 4-0 win over the Red Sox in last year’s Wild Card Series. He allowed five hits, all singles, and walked none. Schlittler threw 11 pitches 100 mph or faster, including six in the first inning.
Schlittler was 14-6 with an AL-best 1.95 ERA and 239 strikeouts this year, the first full season for the 25-year-old right-hander. Schlittler also allowed one earned run or fewer in his final nine starts, matching Whitey Ford in 1963 for the longest streak in Yankees history.
A native of Walpole Massachusetts, Schlittler went 2-1 with an 0.74 ERA in four starts against Boston this year. He struck out 27 in 24 1/3 innings and held hitters to a .174 average.
If the Yankees advance to a best-of-five AL Division Series against Tampa Bay, Schlittler would be lined up to start Game 2 and, if necessary, Game 5.

Yankees news: Aaron Boone makes Bob Nightengale look silly with final playoff decision on Cam Schlittler, Max Fried appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees are set to take on the Boston Red Sox in the playoffs in the Wild Card round. MLB insider Bob Nightengale initially reported that the club was planning on starting Max Fried in Game 1 of the series, with Cam Schlittler getting the start in Game 2. However, manager Aaron Boone decided to do the exact opposite hours after Nightengale's claims.
Reports indicate that the Yankees officially announced that Schlittler will start in Game 1, while Fried will start in Game 2, according to Jorge Castillo of ESPN. It's also said that if the Wild Card series gets to Game 3, then Gerrit Cole will start that contest.
"Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series for the Yankees. Max Fried will start Game 2. Gerrit Cole would get Game 3 if there is one."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Schlittler last took the mound in the Yankees' 6-4 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on September 24. The 25-year-old right-hander only pitched three innings in that contest. He enters the postseason with an American League-best 1.95 ERA and 0.919 WHIP with 239 strikeouts. He also led MLB in starts with 33.
As for Max Fried, he hasn't played since the club's 6-1 loss to the Rays on September 22. While that outing wasn't his best, the 10-year veteran has been consistent throughout the 2026 campaign. He'll play Game 2 of the Wild Card matchup against the Red Sox with a 2.80 ERA and 0.994 WHIP with 104 strikeouts.
The Yankees have one more regular season game against the Baltimore Orioles before the playoffs begin. That contest is currently on a rain delay. The Game 1 postseason matchup agaisnt Boston will take place on Tuesday, September 29.

item.title: [amNewYork] Yankees-Red Sox Wild Card preview: Big questions looming for both NY, Boston | amNewYork
item.dc:creator: Joe Pantorno; Amnewyork
item.description: Another October begins with baseball’s greatest rivalry clashing in the Bronx, as the Yankees host the Boston Red Sox for a second straight year in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series, beginning on Tuesday night. Taking advantage of a significantly subpar American League, the Yankees managed to tread water without Aaron Judge for more than half of the season, finishing second in the East behind the Tampa Bay Rays. Behind them in third were the Red Sox, who fired their manager, Ale
item.content:encoded:
Another October begins with baseball’s greatest rivalry clashing in the Bronx, as the Yankees host the Boston Red Sox for a second straight year in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series, beginning on Tuesday night.
Taking advantage of a significantly subpar American League, the Yankees managed to tread water without Aaron Judge for more than half of the season, finishing second in the East behind the Tampa Bay Rays. Behind them in third were the Red Sox, who fired their manager, Alex Cora, in April following a miserable start, then caught fire in the summer behind a historic 15-game winning streak to grasp onto the No. 2 Wild Card spot and never let go.
The Yankees will hope that history repeats itself in 2026 and that they can find a way to get past their bitter rivals at home, but there are a remarkable number of huge questions looming over this series for both teams that can turn the tide before a single pitch is even thrown.
Let’s take a look.
Will the Judge preside over his court?
The Yankees’ captain and two-time-defending American League MVP missed three months earlier this summer due to a fractured rib, then lasted just seven days before suffering a “moderate” calf strain, as described by manager Aaron Boone.
All signs point to Judge not being a part of New York’s Wild Card roster, which in part was fueled by Boone last week when he said that the team was not planning on the 34-year-old slugger being available. But Judge pushed back on that, saying, “I’m doing everything I can every single day I show up here to get back and be ready to go.”
Boone disclosed on Sunday that Judge has been doing plyometrics and treadmill work, but other than that, “not a whole lot yet.” That certainly does not bode well for his availability, as he would likely be significantly compromised even if he was available.
Who starts Game 1?
In a short, best-of-three series, it’s usually a no-brainer to go with your ace in an attempt to do everything possible to get the quickest advantage possible. That, in turn, would mean Cam Schlittler, who posted one of the greatest single-season stat lines ever by a Yankees pitcher (1.95 ERA, 239 strikeouts), would get the ball for Game 1 on Tuesday, right?
Not so fast, says Boone.
The Yankees’ skipper is considering starting southpaw Max Fried for Game 1, meaning Schlittler would start Game 2 to either clinch or keep his team’s season alive.
In fairness, Fried has been great since returning from the IL in late July. Over his last 10 starts, he has a 2.29 ERA with 54 strikeouts in 51 innings. He has also allowed just one earned run in 11.2 innings against the Red Sox this season.
Schlittler has had mixed results against Boston this year, but most recently went 5.2 shutout frames on Aug. 28 despite walking five. Still, it was his heroics in Game 3 of the Wild Card Series last year that put the young righty on the map, going eight scoreless innings and striking out 12 in what was a 4-0 win.
Carlos Rodon, who has been red-hot to end the season, to the tune of a 1.89 ERA over the last five weeks, should get the ball for a potential Game 3, meaning the struggling Gerrit Cole might not be in the Yankees’ equation until a possible ALDS matchup with the Rays.
Will the Sox be without their biggest bat?
Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras’ career-best season was cut short on Sept. 17 when he was hit on the right hand by a pitch. Not only has he not appeared in a game since, but he recently experienced a setback while taking swings, then divulged that he still cannot grip a bat.
“It’s really concerning,” Contreras told reporters on Thursday. “But at the same time, I’m putting all my effort, and everything I can do, I’m doing it. I don’t know what else to say. I’m working hard with the trainers; the hand is slowly getting better, but I haven’t been able to swing the last two days. I’ll be honest with the team. I know Tuesday is a really important game. It’s a really important series, and I’ll be completely honest with the team.”
The Red Sox are already going to be without Mickey Gasper, who suffered what Red Sox manager Chad Tracy described as a “significant biceps injury” on Friday. The 30-year-old first baseman/catcher/DH had been red-hot as of late, coming out of nowhere to hit 10 home runs with a 1.082 OPS over his last 33 games before the injury. He would have been the obvious Wild Card replacement for Contreras, who owned a .905 OPS with 27 home runs and 81 RBI in 129 games this season.
For more on the Yankees, visit AMNY.com

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Brian Cashman is once again learning the hard way about Yankees' annual trade deadline failures

Walking away from the deadline without a single pitching addition. And yet, that's exactly what Cashman did. For whatever reason, Cashman deemed that the market wasn't right to add reliever depth, despite the fact that the Yankee
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman spent the 2026 trade deadline adding offense. With Aaron Judge still out and Giancarlo Stanton permanently MIA, it made some sense on paper to add bats like Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos.
You know what didn't make sense? Walking away from the deadline without a single pitching addition. And yet, that's exactly what Cashman did. For whatever reason, Cashman deemed that the market wasn't right to add reliever depth, despite the fact that the Yankees have been running arms like Brent Headrick and Fernando Cruz into the ground all season long.
Not surprisingly, Headrick is beginning to show signs of fatigue (he is human, after all), and Cruz is now injured. The Yankees are signing no-name arms to stay afloat, and Cashman deserves blame for this situation. At least New York Post's Joel Sherman is seeing things clearly.
Brian Cashman thought he could get away with Yankees current bullpen
Are Yankees really still hoping that arms like the untrustworthy Luis Gil or the recovering Clarke Schmidt will help make this crisis go away? That's where we're at entering October, and it's sad.
This roster has a ton of talent, and the American League is decidedly weak this season. But since Cashman ignored the pitching staff at the deadline, their World Series chances have no doubt taken a hit.
While the overachieving Tampa Bay Rays held off the Yankees and Red Sox, and New York deserves credit for emerging from the "grave danger zone" of losing ground to Boston, this front office oversight still doomed them to the Wild Card. Cruz's injury alone doesn't prove this, by the way — he'd been awful since the All-Star break. Anyone watching the Yankees has been able to see that their bullpen has slowly been breaking down. It was happening way before the deadline! It's a miracle things aren't much worse.
Fans can't be too shocked at Cashman's performance (or lack thereof). This has become an annual tradition. He makes false assumptions that the Yankees have enough depth in a certain area (oftentimes the pitching staff), and they never do. He hates purchasing insurance, despite evidence to the contrary that this team underachieves in August (almost every year) and enters the playoffs wounded and tired.
Getting to the postseason has never been a problem for the Yankees during the Cashman era. It's the whole advancing once they get there that's been consistently disappointing, and you can trace that back to Cashman's deadline every season.
Max Fried came back earlier than expected. Great! Schmidt vacillated between being close and injured. Splendid! None of that changes the fact that Cashman should have added reinforcements at the deadline and failed to do so. The script is so familiar at this point. Fans just want something different for once.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees-Red Sox Wild Card Series is only four days away, and there are still so many lineup questions on both sides. Entering the weekend, it wasn't even certain that New York and Boston would be the ALWC matchup! There remained a slim chance that these two clubs would avoid each other in the first round entirely. But, with things settled after Game 1 against the Cubs on Friday, we've now got some very interesting personnel narratives to dive into.
On the Red Sox side of things, Willson Contreras' availability for the Wild Card Series is in serious doubt. Since being struck on the hand with a fastball on September 17, Contreras has been doing everything he can to heal, but his body might simply need more time. Luckily for Boston, X-rays revealed no fracture for Contreras, but there's still significant inflammation and a deep bone bruise.
As of Thursday, Contreras wasn't able to swing without pain. There were reports of him choking up at his locker as he dealt with the reality of not being available for the ALWC. So yes -- there seems to be a very real chance that Contreras doesn't play in the series, which leads us to the Yankees side of the equation.
Yankees rumored to be considering Max Fried in Game 1 of ALWC against a Red Sox lineup missing Willson Contreras
If Contreras is out of the picture, the Red Sox's lineup is suddenly missing its most potent right-handed bat. This would ostensibly give the Yankees a greater advantage with a left-handed starter on the mound in Game 1 (in the event that Contreras decides to play later in the series). And according to fresh rumors, New York is indeed considering leaning into that advantage and putting lefty Max Fried on the mound for Game 1.
Jimmy "Jomboy" O'Brien even characterized the Fried-Game 1 plan as "seemingly locked into place", adding that Cam Schlittler would be slated for Game 2 as part of the plan. Jomboy also relayed that he's heard that Giancarlo Stanton will be on the playoff roster, which makes one re-consider the veracity of all of these rumors. Even so, the Fried part in all of this makes sense, especially considering Contreras.
So what do Boone and Matt Blake actually have in mind for Game 1? It's worth noting that Fried has been historically dominant against the Red Sox, boasting a 1.10 ERA in five starts against Boston since he's been with the Yankees.
Schlittler is New York's undeniable ace at the moment and the imminent AL Cy Young, but the Yankees might seriously mess with the Red Sox by throwing Fried out there for Game 1 instead. Doing so would force Boston to employ their iffy platoon depth against a pitcher who has owned the Red Sox every time he's put on his cleats in recent memory.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – A los Yankees les quedan un par de días de calendario, pero los partidos que determinarán cómo se juzga esta temporada no llegarán hasta la próxima semana. Todo lo que ocurra de aquí a entonces es simplemente preparación para la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana.
Con su próximo enfrentamiento de comodines contra los Medias Rojas ya confirmado oficialmente, los Yankees completaron el viernes otras 18 entradas de temporada regular, logrando dividir honores en una doble cartelera tras vencer 6-3 a los Orioles en el Yankee Stadium.
La victoria de Boston sobre los Cachorros en el primer partido de su doble cartelera aseguró el quinto puesto de clasificación y confirmó el duelo contra los Yankees, quienes se quedaron con el cuarto puesto. Será una reedición exacta de la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana del año pasado, que los Yankees ganaron en tres partidos.
"Prefiero mil veces que sea aquí. Lo quiero en el Bronx", dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. "Lo quiero con nuestros aficionados. Creo que, sin duda, existe esa ventaja".
Tras recuperarse de una derrota por 10-2 —sufrida justo después de la ceremonia de homenaje a CC Sabathia en el Monument Park—, Ryan McMahon, Spencer Jones, Anthony Volpe, el puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos y Luis García Jr. impulsaron carreras para los Yankees, que además contaron con una alentadora actuación de relevo de tres entradas y 2/3 por parte de Will Warren.
Los Yankees aún no han anunciado quién abrirá el partido de Comodin del martes contra los Medias Rojas; el coach de lanzadores, Matt Blake, señaló que están evaluando si utilizar a Max Fried con descanso adicional o a Cam Schlittler —principal candidato al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana—, quien llegaría con su descanso habitual para el primer encuentro.
Sin embargo, dado que Gerrit Cole y Carlos Rodón también figuran como posibles abridores para la postemporada, está previsto que Warren pase a desempeñar un papel en el bullpen durante octubre. Como era de esperar, el repertorio de Warren lució mejor desde el bullpen, incluyendo una recta de cuatro costuras que promedió 94.5 mph (0.8 mph más que su promedio de temporada). Warren permitió tres imparables y no otorgó bases por bolas, además de ponchar a siete bateadores.
McMahon inauguró el marcador en la quinta entrada con un doble impulsador ante el abridor de los Orioles, Brandon Young, quien lanzó cinco episodios. Jones conectó un sencillo productor frente a Josh Walker en el sexto inning, y más tarde en esa misma entrada, Volpe bateó un doble de terreno que impulsó dos carreras ante Anthony Núñez.
Ramos y García conectaron sencillos productores en la séptima entrada.

item.title: [mlb.com] Warren dominates out of 'pen in possible preview of playoff role
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch

Everything that transpires between now and then is simply preparation for the American League Wild Card Series.
